# Sets, relations and topology {#sec-sets-relations-topology}

Mathematics starts with sets and the maps between them, continues with the two ways of building new sets, by
gluing elements together and by pairing them, and reaches geometry when a set is given enough structure to speak
of nearness: a topology. This chapter contains those first steps, in four sections. Sets and maps fixes the
vocabulary of elements, images, injective, surjective and bijective maps and inverses. Relations, quotients and
products introduces composition, equivalence relations and quotient sets, and Cartesian products. Topological
spaces defines open sets, continuity and homeomorphisms, and the subspace and quotient topologies. Compact and
connected spaces adds the three global properties, Hausdorff, compact and connected, that the spaces of the later
chapters all share. The reader who knows this material can skim the definitions and try the exercises; every
notion used later is defined here first, and every counting statement is proved. The standard references
are any introductory text on sets and point-set topology; the examples here are drawn from the circle, the sphere
and the rotation group, which recur throughout the book.

## Sets and maps {#sec-sets}

A set is a collection of things, a map a rule assigning to each thing of one set a thing of another. The six
notions of this section, sets, maps, injective, surjective and bijective maps, and inverse maps, are the vocabulary
in which every later definition is phrased. Each definition is followed by three examples of increasing complexity
and three exercises of increasing difficulty with hidden solutions; the counting results of the section are
collected in @prp-count-maps, after the definition of the inverse map.

### Sets

Before anything can be counted, mapped or given a shape, one has to say what a collection of objects is and when
one collection sits inside another. The picture to keep in mind is a bag of labelled items, with no order and no
repetition, together with the smaller bags that can be taken out of it. The first definition fixes this vocabulary
and the two symbols, membership and inclusion, that recur on every page of the book.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-set}
#### Set

A **set** is a collection of distinct objects, its **elements**; $x \in X$ means that $x$ is an element of $X$. A
set $Y$ is a **subset** of $X$, written $Y \subseteq X$, if every element of $Y$ is an element of $X$. The set with
no elements is the **empty set** $\emptyset$, and $|X|$ denotes the number of elements of a finite set.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest sets are those whose elements can be written out in full, so that the size is a matter of counting.
The three sets below are of this kind, and the last of them, the six rotations of a hexagon, is the first
appearance of a set of symmetries, the kind of set on which the groups of later chapters are built.

::: {#exm-set-finite}
#### Finite sets

$\{1, 2, 3\}$ has three elements; $\{0, 2, 4\}$ is a subset of $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$; the set of six rotations of a
regular hexagon by multiples of $60^\circ$ has $|X| = 6$.
:::

Most sets of analysis and physics cannot be listed element by element. The familiar number systems are the standard
infinite sets, and they come with inclusions among them that will be taken for granted throughout; the lists of $n$
real numbers are the coordinate spaces in which every chart of a manifold takes its values.

::: {#exm-set-numbers}
#### Number sets

$\mathbb{Z}$ (integers), $\mathbb{R}$ (real numbers), $\mathbb{C}$ (complex numbers) and $\mathbb{R}^n$ (lists of
$n$ real numbers) are infinite sets, with $\mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{R} \subseteq \mathbb{C}$.
:::

A set can also be specified by a condition rather than by a list or a name: its elements are the points of some
ambient space that satisfy an equation. The circle, the sphere and the rotation group are all described this way,
and this is how they will be handled throughout the book, as subsets of a coordinate space cut out by polynomial
conditions.

::: {#exm-set-geometric}
#### Geometric sets

The circle $S^1 = \{(X, Y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : X^2 + Y^2 = 1\}$ and the sphere $S^2 = \{(X, Y, Z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 :
X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = 1\}$ are subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$ cut out by one equation; the set $SO(3)$ of
rotations of space is a subset of the set of all $3 \times 3$ real matrices, cut out by the conditions
$R^{\mathsf{T}} R = 1$ and $\det R = 1$.
:::

Inclusions between sets are the first relations that need checking rather than assuming, and each failed inclusion
is witnessed by a single element. This exercise runs through the chain of number systems and then through the
circle and the two discs, where the question becomes whether a boundary belongs to a region.

::: {#exr-set-inclusions}
#### Inclusions among familiar sets

Decide which inclusions hold among $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$, the circle
$S^1 \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, the closed disc $D = \{X^2 + Y^2 \leq 1\}$ and the open disc.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\mathbb{N} \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{R} \subseteq \mathbb{C}$, each inclusion
strict ($-1 \notin \mathbb{N}$, $\tfrac12 \notin \mathbb{Z}$, $\sqrt2 \notin \mathbb{Q}$, $i \notin \mathbb{R}$). The
open disc is a subset of the closed disc, and the circle is a subset of the closed disc but disjoint from the open
one: $S^1 \subseteq D$, $S^1 \cap \{X^2 + Y^2 < 1\} = \emptyset$.
:::

Cutting a set out by two conditions at once is intersecting two sets, and the result can be much smaller than
either. The exercise intersects the circle and the sphere with a plane, where the same slicing has very different
outcomes in two and in three dimensions; the circles of latitude obtained here return when the sphere is given
coordinates.

::: {#exr-set-circle-line}
#### A set cut out by two equations

Describe the set of points of the circle $S^1$ that lie on the line $Y = \tfrac12$, and the set of points of the
sphere $S^2$ with $Z = \tfrac12$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On the circle $X^2 + \tfrac14 = 1$ gives $X = \pm\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$: a set of two points. On the sphere $X^2 + Y^2
= \tfrac34$: a circle of radius $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, a set with infinitely many elements. In Sage:

{{< sage exr-set-circle-line >}}

### Maps

With sets in place, the next notion is a rule that sends elements of one set to elements of another. The picture is
a set of arrows, exactly one leaving each point of the domain, and the two subsets attached to such a rule, the
values actually taken and the points sent into a given target region, are the objects in which continuity and
quotients are later phrased.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-map}
#### Map

A **map** $f : X \to Y$ assigns to every element $x$ of the **domain** $X$ exactly one element $f(x)$ of the
**codomain** $Y$. The **image** of $f$ is the subset $\{f(x) : x \in X\} \subseteq Y$ of values actually taken, and
the **preimage** of a subset $V \subseteq Y$ is $f^{-1}(V) = \{x \in X : f(x) \in V\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
When both sets are finite the map is a table, and its image and preimages are read off directly from that table.
The example also gives a first count, the number of all maps between two small sets, which is the first of the
counts collected in @prp-count-maps.

::: {#exm-map-finite}
#### Maps between finite sets

$f : \{1, 2, 3\} \to \{x, y\}$ with $f(1) = f(2) = x$, $f(3) = y$ is a map with image $\{x, y\}$ and preimage
$f^{-1}(\{x\}) = \{1, 2\}$. There are $2^3 = 8$ maps from a three-element set to a two-element set, one choice of
value for each element (@prp-count-maps).
:::

The functions of calculus are maps with the real line as domain, and their images are the ranges one learns to
compute. The second map of this example goes further: it wraps the line around the circle, so that its image is a
curve rather than an interval and its preimages are infinite sets of angles. This wrapping map is the model for
every parametrisation in the book.

::: {#exm-map-functions}
#### Functions and parametrisations

$\cos : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a map with image $[-1, 1]$. The map $\varphi \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$
from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ has image the circle $S^1$: it parametrises the circle, and the preimage of the
single point $(1, 0)$ is the set of multiples of $2\pi$.
:::

Maps need not start from a line or a plane; the domain can itself be a curved set or a set of matrices. The height
function on the sphere and the map that sends a rotation to the point where it moves the north pole are the two
examples from which the coset description of the sphere is built, and both reappear in the exercises that follow.

::: {#exm-map-projection}
#### Projections and the orbit map

The projection $(X, Y, Z) \mapsto Z$ from the sphere to $\mathbb{R}$ (the height function) has image $[-1, 1]$;
the map $g \mapsto g \cdot (0, 0, 1)$, sending a rotation to the point where it moves the north pole, has domain
$SO(3)$ and image the whole sphere.
:::

For $f : \{1, 2, 3, 4\} \to \{a, b, c\}$ with $f(1) = f(3) = a$, $f(2) = c$, $f(4) = a$, find the image of $f$ and
the preimages of $\{a\}$, $\{b\}$ and $\{a, c\}$.

Sage, with the map as a dictionary:

For a function on the real line, images and preimages are computed by solving inequalities rather than by reading a
table. The squaring map is the standard example in which the preimage of an interval splits into two pieces and the
preimage of a point can be empty.

::: {#exr-map-square}
#### Image and preimage of $x \mapsto x^2$

Find the image of $x \mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$, and the preimages of $[1, 4]$ and of $\{-1\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The image is $[0, \infty)$. $x^2 \in [1, 4]$ means $1 \leq |x| \leq 2$, so the preimage is $[-2, -1] \cup [1, 2]$;
the preimage of $\{-1\}$ is empty, since no square is negative. A preimage can be empty, or larger than the set
whose preimage it is.
:::

The same questions make sense for the height function on the sphere, where the answers are regions of a surface
rather than subsets of a line. This exercise produces preimages that are caps, circles and the empty set, and the
circles of latitude among them are the level sets used later to give the sphere coordinates.

::: {#exr-map-height-cap}
#### Preimage of a cap

For the height function $h(X, Y, Z) = Z$ on the sphere, describe the preimages of the interval $(\tfrac12, 1]$, of
the point $0$ and of the interval $[2, 3]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$h^{-1}((\tfrac12, 1])$ is the open cap of points above the plane $Z = \tfrac12$, including the north pole;
$h^{-1}(0)$ is the equator, a circle; $h^{-1}([2, 3])$ is empty, as $|Z| \leq 1$ on the sphere. The level sets
$h^{-1}(c)$ for $-1 < c < 1$ are the circles of latitude, which are used in @sec-charts to see the sphere as a
surface.
:::

Of the maps seen so far, some lose information, sending two points to the same value, and some do not. The first of
the three properties of a map singles out the ones that do not: the picture is a set of arrows with no two
arrowheads meeting, and the equivalent statement in terms of preimages, at most one point over each value, is the
form that will be used in proofs.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-injective}
#### Injective map

A map $f : X \to Y$ is **injective** (one-to-one) if distinct elements have distinct values: $f(x) = f(x')$
implies $x = x'$. Equivalently, every point of $Y$ has at most one preimage.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For maps between finite sets injectivity can be settled by inspection, and the first map in @fig-map-diagram is the
model. The second half of the example is the pigeonhole principle in its simplest form: a set with more elements
cannot be mapped injectively into a set with fewer, which is one of the counts collected in @prp-count-maps.

::: {#exm-injective-finite}
#### On finite sets

The first map of @fig-map-diagram, $1 \mapsto x$, $2 \mapsto y$ into $\{x, y, z\}$, is injective. No map from a
three-element set to a two-element set is injective, because three elements cannot have three distinct values among
two (@prp-count-maps).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-pair-injective-test.sage`; Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-no-injection-test.sage`.

For functions on the real line, injectivity is the question whether a horizontal line can meet the graph twice.
Exponential and square give the two possible answers, and the square's failure, two arguments with the same value,
is the obstruction that later forces coordinates on a sphere to be restricted.

::: {#exm-injective-exp}
#### The exponential

$\exp : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is injective, since $e^{x} = e^{x'}$ forces $x = x'$; $x \mapsto x^2$ is not,
since $(-1)^2 = 1^2$.
:::

:::

The wrapping map of @exm-map-functions is not injective on the whole line, since an angle is only determined up to
multiples of $2\pi$, but it becomes injective once the domain is restricted to an open interval of length $2\pi$.
This restriction is exactly what a chart does, and the example records the reason before manifolds are introduced.

::: {#exm-injective-chart}
#### The angle on an arc

$\varphi \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ is injective on the interval $(0, 2\pi)$, where distinct angles give
distinct points, but not on all of $\mathbb{R}$, where $\varphi$ and $\varphi + 2\pi$ give the same point. Charts
of manifolds (@sec-charts) are injective for exactly this reason: they are restricted to a piece on which
coordinates label points uniquely.
:::

The reader is now asked to settle injectivity for three maps given by their lists of values, and then to count all
injective maps between two small sets. The count is the first instance of the falling factorial, each value having
to avoid the ones already chosen, which @exr-count-general states in general.

::: {#exr-injective-finite-check}
#### Deciding injectivity

Which of the maps $\{1, 2, 3\} \to \{a, b, c, d\}$ given by $(a, b, c)$, $(a, a, b)$, $(d, c, b)$ (the values of
$1, 2, 3$ in order) are injective? Count all the injective maps from a three-element set to a four-element set.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The first and third are injective (distinct values), the second is not ($1$ and $2$ share the value $a$). An
injective map chooses a value for $1$ among $4$, then for $2$ among the $3$ remaining, then for $3$ among $2$:
$4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 = 24$ injective maps. In Sage, by enumeration:

{{< sage exr-injective-finite-check >}}

For a differentiable function a sign condition on the derivative is the practical test for injectivity, since a
strictly increasing function cannot take the same value twice. This exercise applies the test to two cubics, one
that passes and one that fails at three points, and lets Sage find the roots that witness the failure.

::: {#exr-injective-monotone}
#### A strictly increasing function is injective

Show that $f(x) = x^3 + x$ is injective on $\mathbb{R}$, and that $g(x) = x^3 - x$ is not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f'(x) = 3x^2 + 1 > 0$, so $f$ is strictly increasing: $x < x'$ gives $f(x) < f(x')$, and equal values force equal
arguments. For $g$, $g(-1) = g(0) = g(1) = 0$: three arguments with the same value. In Sage, the derivative and the
three roots:

{{< sage exr-injective-monotone >}}
:::

The restriction that rescued the circle parametrisation in @exm-injective-chart has a two-dimensional analogue for
the sphere. Spherical coordinates are injective on an open rectangle of angles but collapse an entire edge of the
closed rectangle to the north pole; the exercise locates the collapse precisely, and that is why the spherical
chart of a later chapter leaves out the poles.

::: {#exr-injective-sphere-parametrisation}
#### Where spherical coordinates are injective

Is $(\theta, \varphi) \mapsto (\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \sin\theta\sin\varphi, \cos\theta)$ injective on $(0, \pi)
\times (0, 2\pi)$? On $[0, \pi] \times [0, 2\pi)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $(0, \pi) \times (0, 2\pi)$ it is: $\cos\theta$ determines $\theta$ in $(0, \pi)$, and then $\sin\theta > 0$ lets
$(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ determine $\varphi$ in $(0, 2\pi)$. On $[0, \pi] \times [0, 2\pi)$ it is not: every
$(0, \varphi)$ is sent to the north pole $(0, 0, 1)$, so the pole has infinitely many preimages. This is why the
spherical chart of @sec-charts excludes the poles.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

:::

The second property of a map looks at the other end of the arrows: whether every point of the codomain is reached.
The picture is that no element of the target is left without an incoming arrow, and the condition is simply that
the image, defined in @def-map, is the whole codomain.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-surjective}
#### Surjective map

A map $f : X \to Y$ is **surjective** (onto) if its image is all of $Y$: every $y \in Y$ equals $f(x)$ for at
least one $x$.
:::

at least once. The cube, the square and the exponential give three different images, and comparing them with
@exm-injective-exp shows that injectivity and surjectivity are independent properties.

$x \mapsto x^3$ is surjective onto $\mathbb{R}$ (every real number has a cube root); $x \mapsto x^2$ is not (its

The wrapping map onto the circle and the orbit map onto the sphere reach every point of their targets, so they are
surjective even though neither is injective. The surjectivity of the orbit map is what allows the sphere to be
described as a quotient of the rotation group, the theme that @sec-relations-products takes up.

::: {#exm-surjective-orbit}
#### Parametrisations and orbit maps

$\varphi \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ is surjective from $\mathbb{R}$ onto the circle, and $g \mapsto g \cdot
(0, 0, 1)$ is surjective from $SO(3)$ onto the sphere, since every point of the sphere is reached by some rotation
of the north pole. This surjection is the starting point of the coset description of the sphere
(@sec-coset-spaces).
:::

Whether a map is surjective depends on the codomain declared for it, not on the rule alone. This exercise asks for
the images of two familiar functions and then for the codomains onto which they are surjective, making the point
that any map becomes surjective once its codomain is shrunk to its image.

::: {#exr-surjective-sin}
#### The image of a function

Find the image of $\sin : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and of $x \mapsto x^2 + 1$; onto which codomains are they
surjective?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sin$ has image $[-1, 1]$: it is surjective onto $[-1, 1]$ but not onto $\mathbb{R}$. $x^2 + 1$ has image
$[1, \infty)$. Surjectivity depends on the codomain chosen: every map is surjective onto its image.
:::

The orbit maps of @exm-surjective-orbit behave differently in the plane and in space, and the exercise asks the
reader to find out how. For plane rotations acting on a point of the circle the orbit map is a bijection, while in
space every point of the sphere has a whole circle of rotations above it; these preimages are the first cosets of
the book.

::: {#exr-surjective-rotation-orbit}
#### A surjection with equal-size preimages

Show that $g \mapsto g \cdot (1, 0)$ from $SO(2)$, the rotations of the plane, onto the circle is a bijection, and
that $g \mapsto g \cdot (0, 0, 1)$ from $SO(3)$ onto the sphere has, for every point, a preimage that is a copy of
$SO(2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A plane rotation by $\alpha$ sends $(1, 0)$ to $(\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha)$, each point of the circle once: a
bijection. In space, the rotations sending the pole to a given point $p$ are $g_0 h$ with $g_0$ one such rotation
and $h$ any rotation about the $Z$-axis, which fixes the pole: the preimage of $p$ is a copy of $SO(2)$. These
preimages are the cosets of @sec-cosets-quotients.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

A map with both properties sets up a perfect correspondence: every element of the target is hit, and hit exactly
once. The picture is a pairing of the two sets, arrow by arrow, and the consequence recorded in the definition,
that paired sets have the same number of elements, is the basis of every count in this section.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-bijection}
#### Bijection

A map is a **bijection** if it is both injective and surjective, so that every element of $Y$ is the value of
exactly one element of $X$. Two sets related by a bijection have the same number of elements.
:::

element fixed. The second count shows how the permutations of a smaller set sit inside those of a larger one, and

$4! = 24$ bijections; those fixing $4$ are the $3! = 6$ permutations of $\{1, 2, 3\}$. In Sage, with

For a function given by a formula, the cleanest proof that it is a bijection is to solve $f(x) = y$ and find
exactly one solution for each $y$. The exercise does this for an affine map of the line, and then shows that the
same formula, read on the integers, loses surjectivity: the domain matters as much as the rule.

::: {#exr-bijection-affine}
#### An affine bijection

Show that $f(x) = 2x + 1$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{R}$ by exhibiting the unique solution of $f(x) = y$ for each
$y$, and decide whether $x \mapsto 2x + 1$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{Z}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$2x + 1 = y$ has the unique real solution $x = (y - 1)/2$, so $f$ is injective (one solution at most) and
surjective (one solution at least). On $\mathbb{Z}$ the equation has no solution for even $y$: the map is
injective but not surjective, its image being the odd integers.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-affine-solution-test.sage`; Recipe `ideal_membership`, certificate `ideal_membership.sage`; Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-int-affine-test.sage`.

**Lean.**

Stereographic projection sends the sphere minus one point onto the whole plane, and the exercise asks for a proof
that this is a bijection by writing down the inverse. The explicit formula found here is the second chart of the
sphere used throughout the book, and Sage checks both compositions symbolically.

::: {#exr-bijection-stereographic}
#### Stereographic projection is a bijection

Show that $(X, Y, Z) \mapsto (X, Y)/(1 - Z)$ is a bijection from the sphere minus the north pole onto the plane,
by finding its inverse.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $(u, v)$ in the plane, the point $(2u, 2v, u^2 + v^2 - 1)/(u^2 + v^2 + 1)$ lies on the sphere, is not the north
pole, and projects to $(u, v)$; conversely projecting and then applying this formula returns the original point.
Sage checks both compositions:

{{< sage exr-bijection-stereographic >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Recipe `ideal_membership`, certificate `ideal_membership.sage`.

The exercises above all proved bijectivity by exhibiting a map that undoes the given one. That undoing map is the
subject of the next definition: the picture is the arrows of a bijection reversed, and the two identities in the
definition say that going there and back, in either order, changes nothing.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-inverse-map}
#### Inverse map

The **inverse** of a bijection $f : X \to Y$ is the map $f^{-1} : Y \to X$ sending $y$ to the unique $x$ with $f(x)
= y$; it satisfies $f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$ and $f(f^{-1}(y)) = y$. Only bijections have inverses.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-has-inverse-test.sage`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Sets.Inverse.bijective_iff_has_inverse >}}

**Sage.** `set-has-inverse-test.sage` instances `(X = Fin 2, Y = Fin 2, f = id)`, `(X = ℤ, Y = ℤ, f = fun k => k + 1)`, `(X = Fin 3, Y = Fin 2, f = ![0, 0, 1])`.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On a finite set with modular addition, the inverse of a shift is the shift in the opposite direction, while a map
that is not a bijection, such as doubling, has no inverse at all. The shift's bijectivity is the fourth
statement of @prp-count-maps.

::: {#exm-inverse-shift}
#### The shift of $\mathbb{Z}_6$

$k \mapsto k + 1$ on $\{0, \dots, 5\}$ with addition modulo $6$ is a bijection with inverse $k \mapsto k - 1$
(@prp-count-maps); $k \mapsto 2k$ is not a bijection, as it sends both $0$ and $3$ to $0$, so it has no inverse.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

:::

The inverses of the bijections of the line in @exm-bijection-cube are functions with their own names. Logarithm,
arctangent and cube root are the standard examples, and each is defined on exactly the image of the function it
inverts.

::: {#exm-inverse-log}
#### Logarithm and arctangent

The inverse of $\exp : \mathbb{R} \to (0, \infty)$ is $\log$; the inverse of $\tan : (-\pi/2, \pi/2) \to \mathbb{R}$
is $\arctan$; the inverse of $x \mapsto x^3$ is the cube root.
:::

For rotations, the inverse is geometric: turning back by the same angle, which for matrices is the transpose. The
example also returns to the angle labelling of the circle from @exm-bijection-chart and identifies its inverse as
the chart that reads off the angle of a point.

::: {#exm-inverse-rotation}
#### Rotations

A rotation by the angle $\alpha$ about an axis is a bijection of space whose inverse is the rotation by $-\alpha$
about the same axis; as a matrix, $R^{-1} = R^{\mathsf{T}}$. The inverse of the coordinate bijection of
@exm-bijection-chart sends a point of the circle to its angle in $(0, 2\pi)$, which is the chart itself.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise asks the reader to verify the claims of @exm-inverse-shift on $\mathbb{Z}_6$: produce the
inverse of the shift and show that doubling has none. Exhibiting an inverse that undoes the map in both orders is
the quickest proof of bijectivity, and it is the argument behind the last count of @prp-count-maps.

::: {#exr-inverse-check}
#### Inverse of a bijection

Show that $k \mapsto k + 1$ on $\mathbb{Z}_6$ is a bijection and give its inverse; show that $k \mapsto 2k$ is not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$k \mapsto k - 1$ undoes the shift in both orders, so the shift is a bijection. Doubling sends $0$ and $3$ both to
$0$, so it is not injective, and its image $\{0, 2, 4\}$ is not all of $\mathbb{Z}_6$, so it is not surjective
either.
:::

Finding an inverse of a rational function means solving for $x$ in terms of $y$ and keeping track of which values
have to be excluded on each side. The exercise does this for a simple Möbius transformation and asks for a check of
the composition, which Sage carries out.

::: {#exr-inverse-moebius}
#### Inverting a rational function

Find the inverse of $f(x) = \dfrac{x - 1}{x + 1}$ on its natural domain and codomain, and check $f(f^{-1}(y)) = y$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Solving $y = (x - 1)/(x + 1)$ gives $x = (1 + y)/(1 - y)$, so $f$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{-1\}$
onto $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{1\}$ with that inverse. In Sage, both compositions:

{{< sage exr-inverse-moebius >}}
:::

The statement in @exm-inverse-rotation that a rotation is undone by its transpose is checked here for a rotation
about the $Z$-axis. The proof uses only the addition formulas for sine and cosine and the parity of those
functions, and Sage does it symbolically.

::: {#exr-inverse-rotation-matrix}
#### The inverse of a rotation is its transpose

For the rotation matrix $R(\alpha)$ about the $Z$-axis, verify $R(\alpha)^{-1} = R(-\alpha) = R(\alpha)^{\mathsf{T}}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$R(\alpha)R(-\alpha) = 1$ by the addition formulas for sine and cosine, and $R(-\alpha)$ is the transpose because
$\cos$ is even and $\sin$ odd. In Sage, symbolically:

{{< sage exr-inverse-rotation-matrix >}}

Several counts have been stated in the examples: eight maps from three elements to two, none of them injective, six
bijections of a three-element set, and the shift of $\mathbb{Z}_6$ as a bijection. The proposition collects them,
and the three examples that follow explain the first three counts by arguments that work for sets of any size.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-count-maps}
#### Counting maps

There are $8$ maps from a three-element set to a two-element set, none of them injective; there are $6$
bijections of a three-element set; and $k \mapsto k + 1$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{Z}_6$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first of the four counts has a conceptual explanation: a map from a three-element set is the list of its
values, so the maps form a threefold product of the codomain with itself. The same argument counts the maps
between any two finite sets, and it anticipates the products of @def-product.

::: {#exm-count-product}
#### Eight maps as a product

A map $\{1, 2, 3\} \to \{x, y\}$ is the list of its three values, an element of $\{x, y\}^3$ with $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2
= 8$ elements (@def-product). In general the maps $X \to Y$ between finite sets number $|Y|^{|X|}$.
:::

The count of bijections comes from a tree of successive choices, each with one fewer option than the last.
Following this tree down to its leaves gives the factorial, and the same tree on $n$ elements gives $n!$
bijections.

::: {#exm-count-factorial}
#### Six bijections by a tree

Choose the value of $1$ ($3$ ways), then of $2$ ($2$ remaining), then of $3$ ($1$ remaining): $3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 =
3! = 6$ bijections.
:::

The negative statement among the four, that no injection exists from three elements to two, is the pigeonhole
principle. It follows from the inequality between the sizes of the domain and the codomain of an injective map,
the form in which the principle is used in every later counting argument.

::: {#exm-count-pigeonhole}
#### No injection from three to two

Three distinct values cannot fit in a two-element set: this is the pigeonhole principle, which follows from the
inequality $|X| \leq |Y|$ for an injective map $X \to Y$.
:::

The last exercise of the section asks for the closed formulas behind the special cases: the number of maps,
injections and bijections between finite sets of sizes $m$ and $n$. The arguments of the three examples above
transfer verbatim, and the result contains the counts of @prp-count-maps as special cases.

::: {#exr-count-general}
#### The general formulas

For finite sets with $|X| = m$ and $|Y| = n$, give the number of maps $X \to Y$, of injective maps, and of
bijections, and prove them by the counting arguments of the examples.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Maps: $n^m$ (independent choices). Injective maps: $n(n - 1)\cdots(n - m + 1)$ for $m \leq n$ and $0$ for $m > n$
(each value must avoid the previous ones). Bijections: $n!$ when $m = n$ and $0$ otherwise. The first three
counts of @prp-count-maps are the instances $2^3 = 8$, no injection for $m = 3 > n = 2$, and $3! = 6$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

## Relations, quotients and products {#sec-relations-products}

Maps are combined by composition, and sets are built from other sets in two ways: by gluing elements together
(quotients) and by pairing them (products). An equivalence relation says which elements are to be identified, its
classes are the glued-together pieces, and the quotient set is the set of pieces; a product pairs an element of one
set with an element of another. The section defines composition, equivalence relations, classes, quotient sets and
products, with the remainders modulo $n$, the angles on a circle and the rotations with a common image of the pole
as running examples.

### Composition

Two maps whose domains and codomains fit together can be performed one after the other, and the result is a single
map. The picture is a chain of arrows followed from end to end, and the identity map and the inverse of
@def-inverse-map find their natural statements here, as the map that composes to nothing and the map that composes
to the identity.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-composition}
#### Composition of maps

The **composition** of $f : X \to Y$ and $g : Y \to Z$ is the map $g \circ f : X \to Z$, $x \mapsto g(f(x))$:
first $f$, then $g$. The **identity map** $\mathrm{id}_X : X \to X$ sends every element to itself, and
a bijection $f$ and its inverse (@def-inverse-map) satisfy $f^{-1} \circ f = \mathrm{id}_X$, $f \circ f^{-1} =
\mathrm{id}_Y$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-inverse-comp-test.sage`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Sets.Composition.inverse_comp >}}

**Sage.** `set-inverse-comp-test.sage` instances `(X = Fin 3, Y = Fin 3, e = Equiv.refl _)`, `(X = Fin 3, Y = Fin 3, e = finRotate 3)`, `(X = ℤ, Y = ℤ, e = Equiv.addRight 1)`.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Composing permutations of a small set is the first place where the order of composition visibly matters. A swap
followed by a cycle differs from the cycle followed by the swap, and this failure of commutativity is what makes
the symmetric groups and the rotation groups of later chapters non-abelian.

::: {#exm-composition-permutations}
#### Permutations

For the swap $s$ of $1$ and $2$ and the cycle $t : 1 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 1$ of $\{1, 2, 3\}$, the two
compositions $t \circ s$ and $s \circ t$ are different permutations: composition is not commutative in general
(@exr-compose-permutations).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Recipe `witness`, certificate `set-perm-noncommute.sage`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Sets.Composition.swap_cycle_noncommute >}}

**Sage.** `set-perm-noncommute.sage`: Sage composes s and t in both orders (as functions, first s then t, and first t then s) and returns a point where they differ, shifted to 0-based labels. .
:::

Composing a coordinate bijection with the inverse of another produces the map that converts one set of coordinates
into the other. For the two stereographic charts of the sphere this conversion is an inversion of the punctured
plane, the first concrete instance of the compatibility condition that defines a manifold.

::: {#exm-composition-transition}
#### Transition maps

Two coordinate bijections $x$ and $x'$ on overlapping pieces of a space are composed into $x' \circ x^{-1}$, the
**transition map** of @sec-charts. For the two stereographic charts of the sphere it is the inversion
$(u, v) \mapsto (u, v)/(u^2 + v^2)$ of the punctured plane, which is its own inverse.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Recipe `ideal_membership`, certificate `ideal_membership.sage`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Sets.Composition.transition_inversion >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Sets.Composition.inversion_involutive >}}

**Sage.** `ideal_membership.sage`: Write lhs - rhs as a combination of the equality hypotheses; linear_combination checks it. .
:::

For rotations, composition is the operation on which the whole of group theory is built: performing one rotation
after another. About a common axis the angles simply add, while about different axes the order matters, exactly as
for the permutations of @exm-composition-permutations; @exr-compose-rotations-noncommute makes this concrete.

::: {#exm-composition-rotations}
#### Rotations

Composing a rotation by $\alpha$ with a rotation by $\beta$ about the same axis is the rotation by $\alpha + \beta$;
for rotations about different axes the order matters, as for permutations. Composition is the multiplication of
the groups of @sec-groups.
:::

Composition is not commutative, but it is associative: the two bracketings of a triple composition describe the
same rule. The exercise asks for the short proof and for a numerical check on random permutations, the first of the
group axioms to be verified in this book.

::: {#exr-compose-associative}
#### Associativity

Show that composition is associative, $(h \circ g) \circ f = h \circ (g \circ f)$, and check it on three random
permutations of $\{1, \dots, 5\}$.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both sides send $x$ to $h(g(f(x)))$: the two bracketings describe the same rule, so they are the same map. In
Sage, three random permutations:

{{< sage exr-compose-associative >}}

### Equivalence relations and quotients

The first way of building a new set from an old one is to declare certain elements to be the same. The declaration
has to be consistent, and the three axioms of the next definition say exactly what consistency means: every element
is like itself, likeness is mutual, and likeness is passed along a chain.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-equivalence-relation}
#### Equivalence relation

An **equivalence relation** $\sim$ on $X$ is a relation between elements that is **reflexive** ($x \sim x$),
**symmetric** ($x \sim y$ implies $y \sim x$) and **transitive** ($x \sim y$ and $y \sim z$ imply $x \sim z$).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Congruence of integers is the basic example: two integers are alike when their difference is a multiple of a fixed
$n$. The three axioms translate into three facts about divisibility, each one line long, and this relation is the
source of the finite sets $\mathbb{Z}_n$.

::: {#exm-equivalence-mod}
#### Congruence modulo $n$

$a \sim b$ if $n$ divides $a - b$ is an equivalence relation on $\mathbb{Z}$: $n$ divides $0$, divides $b - a$ if
it divides $a - b$, and divides $(a - b) + (b - c)$ if it divides both terms.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-modeq-equivalence-test.sage`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Sets.Equivalence.modEq_equivalence >}}

**Sage.** `set-modeq-equivalence-test.sage` instances `(n = 3)`, `(n = 0)`, `(n = 2)`.
:::

Replacing the integer $n$ by the real number $2\pi$ gives the relation that identifies angles differing by full
turns. It is the same congruence in a continuous setting, and it is the relation whose classes are glued into the
circle in @fig-quotient-circle.

::: {#exm-equivalence-angle}
#### Angles

$\varphi \sim \varphi'$ if $\varphi' - \varphi$ is a multiple of $2\pi$ is an equivalence relation on $\mathbb{R}$,
the congruence of @exm-equivalence-mod with $n$ replaced by $2\pi$; it identifies the angles that label the same
point of the circle (@fig-quotient-circle).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

Every map produces an equivalence relation on its domain, relating points that share a value, and the axioms hold
automatically. For the orbit map on the rotation group this relation groups together the rotations that move the
north pole to the same place, and its classes are the cosets around which the coset spaces of the book are
organised.

::: {#exm-equivalence-coset}
#### Same image under a map

For any map $f : X \to Y$, $x \sim x'$ if $f(x) = f(x')$ is an equivalence relation. For the orbit map $g \mapsto g
\cdot (0, 0, 1)$ on $SO(3)$ it relates two rotations that send the north pole to the same point; this relation is
the one whose classes are the cosets of @sec-cosets-quotients.
:::

Testing the three axioms on a finite set is a finite job, and the exercise asks for it on three relations chosen so
that a different axiom fails in each case that fails. Sage runs through all pairs and triples, which is the
mechanical version of the same check.

::: {#exr-equivalence-check}
#### Which relations are equivalence relations?

On $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, test the three axioms for the relations "$a \sim b$ iff $a - b$ is even", "$a \sim b$ iff
$a \leq b$" and "$a \sim b$ iff $|a - b| \leq 1$".
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Same parity: reflexive, symmetric, transitive. $\leq$: reflexive and transitive but not symmetric ($1 \leq 2$,
$2 \not\leq 1$). $|a - b| \leq 1$: reflexive and symmetric but not transitive ($1 \sim 2$, $2 \sim 3$, $1 \not\sim
3$). Sage tests the axioms on all pairs and triples:

{{< sage exr-equivalence-check >}}
:::

The parity relation is congruence modulo $2$, and the exercise asks the reader to prove the three axioms rather
than test them. The companion relation, differing by an odd number, fails already at reflexivity, a reminder that
the first axiom is not automatic.

::: {#exr-equivalence-parity}
#### Same parity

Prove that "$a \sim b$ iff $a - b$ is even" is an equivalence relation on $\mathbb{Z}$, and that "$a \sim b$ iff
$a - b$ is odd" is not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$a - a = 0$ is even; if $a - b$ is even so is $b - a = -(a - b)$; if $a - b$ and $b - c$ are even so is their sum
$a - c$. For the odd relation, $a - a = 0$ is not odd, so reflexivity already fails (and transitivity too: odd plus
odd is even).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

Being within distance one of each other is a natural relation that fails to be an equivalence relation, and the
exercise asks why, and what the smallest equivalence relation containing it looks like. The answer depends on
whether the underlying set is in one piece, a first glimpse of connectedness.

::: {#exr-equivalence-closeness}
#### Closeness is not transitive

Explain why "$x \sim y$ iff $|x - y| < 1$" is not an equivalence relation on $\mathbb{R}$, and find the smallest
relation containing it that is one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Transitivity fails: $0 \sim 0.9$ and $0.9 \sim 1.8$ but $|0 - 1.8| \geq 1$. Chaining closeness, any two real
numbers are joined by finitely many steps of length less than $1$, so the smallest equivalence relation containing
it relates every pair: one class, all of $\mathbb{R}$. On a disconnected set like $(0, 1) \cup (5, 6)$ the chains
cannot cross the gap and there would be two classes (@sec-compact-connected).
:::

Once an equivalence relation is given, each element gathers around it the elements it is related to. The next
definition names this cluster and records its key property: two clusters are either identical or disjoint, so that
the set falls apart into non-overlapping pieces. The picture is a tiling of the set.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-equivalence-class}
#### Equivalence class

The **equivalence class** of $x$ is the subset $[x] = \{y \in X : y \sim x\}$. Two classes are either equal or
disjoint, so the classes **partition** $X$: every element lies in exactly one class.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

#### Remainders

Modulo $3$, the classes in $\{0, \dots, 11\}$ are $\{0, 3, 6, 9\}$, $\{1, 4, 7, 10\}$ and $\{2, 5, 8, 11\}$, the
numbers with remainder $0$, $1$, $2$: three disjoint sets covering everything (@exr-equivalence-classes).

For the angle relation each class is an arithmetic progression of step $2\pi$, with exactly one representative in
every interval of that length. The three coloured classes in @fig-quotient-circle are of this kind, and the picture
shows how each class is about to become a single point.

::: {#exm-class-angle}
#### Classes of angles

The class of $\varphi$ under the angle relation is $\{\varphi + 2\pi k : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$, one angle in every
interval of length $2\pi$; @fig-quotient-circle shows three such classes on the line in three colours.
:::

For the relation of @exm-equivalence-coset on the rotation group, the class of a rotation is obtained by first
turning about the axis through the pole and then applying the rotation. Such a class is a copy of the plane
rotations, and the notation $g\,SO(2)$ for it is the coset notation of the group chapters.

::: {#exm-class-rotations}
#### Rotations with the same image of the pole

The class of a rotation $g$ under the relation of @exm-equivalence-coset is the set $\{g h : h \text{ a rotation
about the } Z\text{-axis}\}$: rotating first about the $Z$-axis leaves the north pole fixed, so $gh$ sends it where
$g$ does. These classes are the cosets $g\,SO(2)$.
:::

The reader is asked to compute the classes of @exm-class-mod and to check that they form a partition. The Sage
enumeration here is the model for computing the classes of any relation on a finite set.

::: {#exr-equivalence-classes}
#### Classes modulo 3

List the equivalence classes of $n \sim m$ iff $3 \mid (n - m)$ on $\{0, \dots, 11\}$ and check that they
partition the set.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Three classes, the numbers with remainder $0$, $1$ and $2$: $\{0, 3, 6, 9\}$, $\{1, 4, 7, 10\}$, $\{2, 5, 8, 11\}$,
disjoint and covering the set. In Sage:

{{< sage exr-equivalence-classes >}}
:::

Relations of the form "same value under a map" have classes equal to the preimages of the values, and the exercise
computes them for the square and for the cosine. In each case most classes have the same size and a few are
exceptional, a phenomenon that recurs for quotients by group actions.

::: {#exr-class-square}
#### Classes of "same square"

Describe the classes of $x \sim y$ iff $x^2 = y^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$, and the classes of "same value of $\cos$".
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[x] = \{x, -x\}$, a two-element class for $x \neq 0$ and the single element $\{0\}$ for $x = 0$: the quotient is
labelled by $|x|$. For $\cos$, $[x] = \{\pm x + 2\pi k\}$: the quotient is labelled by $\cos x \in [-1, 1]$, and a
class has two elements per period except for $x \in \pi\mathbb{Z}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The partition property stated in @def-equivalence-class deserves a proof, and the exercise asks for it. The
argument is a short chain of symmetry and transitivity, and it is exactly what makes the quotient set of the next
definition well defined.

::: {#exr-class-partition-proof}
#### Classes are equal or disjoint

Prove that if two equivalence classes $[x]$ and $[y]$ share an element then $[x] = [y]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $z \in [x] \cap [y]$, so $z \sim x$ and $z \sim y$. For any $w \in [x]$, $w \sim x \sim z \sim y$ by symmetry and
transitivity, so $w \in [y]$; the same argument in the other direction gives $[y] \subseteq [x]$. Every $x$ lies in
$[x]$ by reflexivity, so the classes cover $X$: they partition it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-classes-partition-test.sage`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Sets.Equivalence.classes_partition >}}

**Sage.** `set-classes-partition-test.sage` instances `(X = ℤ, s = ⟨fun a b => (3 : ℤ) ∣ a - b, KaluzaKlein.Sets.Equivalence.modEq_equivalence 3⟩, x = 1, y = 4)`, `(X = Unit, s = ⊥, x = (), y = ())`, `(X = ℤ, s = ⟨fun a b => (3 : ℤ) ∣ a - b, KaluzaKlein.Sets.Equivalence.modEq_equivalence 3⟩, x = 0, y = 2)`.
:::
::::

The classes of an equivalence relation can now be taken as the elements of a new set, the set of tiles of the
partition. The next definition introduces this set together with the map that sends each element to its tile, and
with the criterion for a function on the old set to make sense on the new one: it has to take the same value
throughout each tile.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-quotient-set}
#### Quotient set

The **quotient set** $X/{\sim}$ is the set whose elements are the equivalence classes. The **quotient map**
$\pi : X \to X/{\sim}$, $x \mapsto [x]$, is surjective, and a map $f : X \to Y$ that is constant on each class
**descends** to the map $\bar f : X/{\sim} \to Y$, $[x] \mapsto f(x)$, with $f = \bar f \circ \pi$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-quotient-descends-test.sage`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Sets.Quotients.quotient_descends >}}

**Sage.** `set-quotient-descends-test.sage` instances `(X = ℤ, Y = ℤ, s = ⟨fun a b => (3 : ℤ) ∣ a - b, KaluzaKlein.Sets.Equivalence.modEq_equivalence 3⟩, f = fun a => a % 3)`, `(X = Unit, Y = Unit, s = ⊥, f = id)`, `(X = ℝ, Y = ℝ, s = ⟨fun a b : ℝ => ∃ k : ℤ, b - a = k * (2 * Real.pi), KaluzaKlein.Sets.Equivalence.angle_equivalence _⟩, f = Real.cos)`.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The quotient of the integers by congruence modulo $n$ is the finite set of remainders, and addition descends to it
because the remainder of a sum depends only on the remainders of the summands. Its size is the statement of
@prp-quotient-z3, and the addition makes it the cyclic group of the group chapters.

::: {#exm-quotient-zn}
#### $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$

The quotient of $\mathbb{Z}$ by congruence modulo $n$ is the set $\mathbb{Z}_n$ of $n$ remainders
(@prp-quotient-z3); addition descends to it, since the remainder of a sum depends only on the remainders of the
terms, giving the group $\mathbb{Z}_n$ of @sec-groups.
:::

The quotient of the line by the angle relation is the circle, each class of angles collapsing to one point as in
@fig-quotient-circle. The functions that descend to the circle are exactly the $2\pi$-periodic ones, which is the
criterion of @def-quotient-set made concrete; @exr-descend tests it on three functions.

::: {#exm-quotient-circle}
#### The circle as a quotient

$\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, the quotient by the angle relation, is the circle: the class of $\varphi$ corresponds to
the point $(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ (@fig-quotient-circle). $\cos$ and $\sin$ descend to the circle, being
$2\pi$-periodic, while $\varphi \mapsto \varphi$ does not.
:::

The quotient of the rotation group by the relation "same image of the pole" is the sphere, since a class is
determined by where it sends the pole and every point is reached. This is the set-theoretic content of the
statement $S^2 = SO(3)/SO(2)$, whose topological version appears in @exm-quotient-sphere-top.

::: {#exm-quotient-sphere}
#### The sphere as a quotient of the rotation group

The quotient of $SO(3)$ by the relation of @exm-equivalence-coset is the sphere: the class of $g$ is determined by
the point $g \cdot (0, 0, 1)$, and every point arises. This is the coset space $SO(3)/SO(2)$ of @sec-coset-spaces.
:::

The reader is asked to check that addition is well defined on the classes modulo $5$, which is the descent
criterion of @def-quotient-set for a function of two arguments. Writing out the table, with Sage's help, shows the
finite group that results.

::: {#exr-quotient-z5-table}
#### Addition on $\mathbb{Z}_5$

Write the addition table of $\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}$ and check that addition is well defined on classes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Well defined: if $a \equiv a'$ and $b \equiv b'$ modulo $5$ then $a + b \equiv a' + b'$, since $(a + b) - (a' + b')
= (a - a') + (b - b')$ is a multiple of $5$. The table, from Sage's `Zmod(5)`:

Which functions of an angle are really functions of a point on the circle? The exercise answers this for three
candidates, and the test is simply periodicity, since a function descends to the quotient exactly when it is
constant on the classes.

::: {#exr-descend}
#### Which functions descend to the circle?

Decide which of $\varphi \mapsto \cos 2\varphi$, $\varphi \mapsto \cos(\varphi/2)$ and $\varphi \mapsto e^{i\varphi}$
descend from $\mathbb{R}$ to the quotient $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A function descends exactly when it is constant on classes, that is, $2\pi$-periodic. $\cos 2\varphi$ and
$e^{i\varphi}$ are $2\pi$-periodic and descend; $\cos(\varphi/2)$ changes sign under $\varphi \mapsto \varphi +
2\pi$ and does not. Sage checks periodicity symbolically:

{{< sage exr-descend >}}
:::

Equivalence relations can glue geometric figures too, and the exercise glues the opposite edges of a square.
Counting the elements in the classes of corners, edge points and interior points shows the structure of the
resulting surface, which @exm-quotient-torus identifies as the torus.

::: {#exr-quotient-square}
#### Gluing the edges of a square

Identify the opposite edges of the square $[0, 1]^2$: $(0, v) \sim (1, v)$ and $(u, 0) \sim (u, 1)$. How many
classes do the four corners form? Which points of the square have classes with exactly two elements?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The four corners are all identified: $(0, 0) \sim (1, 0) \sim (1, 1) \sim (0, 1)$, one class. Points in the interior
of an edge have two-element classes, $\{(0, v), (1, v)\}$ or $\{(u, 0), (u, 1)\}$; interior points are alone in their
class. The quotient is the torus (@exm-quotient-torus): a surface with one vertex, two edges and one face.
:::

### Products

The second way of building a new set pairs an element of one set with an element of another, with no identification
at all. The picture is a rectangle whose rows are indexed by one set and whose columns are indexed by the other,
and the two projections of the definition read off the row and the column of a pair.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-product}
#### Cartesian product

The **Cartesian product** $X \times Y$ is the set of ordered pairs $(x, y)$ with $x \in X$ and $y \in Y$; it has
$|X| \cdot |Y|$ elements when both sets are finite. The **projections** $(x, y) \mapsto x$ and $(x, y) \mapsto y$
are surjective maps onto the factors, and $X \times Y \times Z$ is the set of triples.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Sets.Products.projections_surjective >}}

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The coordinate spaces are products of copies of the line, which is why a point of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a list of $n$
numbers. The torus is the product of two circles, and the example makes the point that a product space is labelled
by pairs of labels of its factors.

::: {#exm-product-rn}
#### $\mathbb{R}^n$ and the torus

$\mathbb{R}^n = \mathbb{R} \times \dots \times \mathbb{R}$ with $n$ factors; the torus $T^2 = S^1 \times S^1$ is the
set of pairs of points of the circle, which is why a point of the torus is labelled by a pair of angles.
:::

Products are how physics combines independent degrees of freedom: the configuration space of two systems is the
product of their configuration spaces. The example lists two mechanical instances and then the one that drives this
book, a spacetime with extra dimensions as a product of ordinary spacetime with an internal space.

::: {#exm-product-spacetime}
#### Product spaces in physics

The configuration space of two particles on a line is $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$, of a particle on a circle
and one on a sphere $S^1 \times S^2$; the spacetimes with extra dimensions of Parts III to V are products $M_4
\times K$ of spacetime with an internal space, a point being a pair (spacetime point, internal point).
:::

The count of maps from a three-element set in @exm-count-product was really a statement about products, and the
example makes the identification explicit. A map out of a finite set is a tuple of values, that is, an element of a
product of copies of the codomain.

::: {#exm-product-maps}
#### Counting maps as a product

A map from $\{1, 2, 3\}$ to $\{x, y\}$ is the triple of its values, an element of $\{x, y\} \times \{x, y\} \times
\{x, y\}$, which has $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8$ elements: this is how @exr-count-maps enumerates the maps.
:::

A point of the torus is a pair of angles, and the exercise asks for the point corresponding to one particular pair,
first in the product description inside $\mathbb{R}^4$ and then on the familiar doughnut surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
Comparing the two coordinate descriptions of the same point shows that the product and the surface of revolution
are two pictures of one set.

::: {#exr-product-torus-point}
#### A point of the torus from two angles

Give the point of $T^2 = S^1 \times S^1 \subset \mathbb{R}^4$ with angles $(\pi/3, \pi/2)$, and the point of the
torus embedded in $\mathbb{R}^3$ as a surface of revolution with the same angles.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In $\mathbb{R}^4$: $(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{3}, \sin\tfrac{\pi}{3}, \cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}) = (\tfrac12,
\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, 0, 1)$. In $\mathbb{R}^3$ with radii $2$ and $1$: $((2 + \cos v)\cos u, (2 + \cos v)\sin u, \sin v)$ at
$(u, v) = (\pi/3, \pi/2)$ gives $(1, \sqrt3, 1)$. Sage evaluates both:

{{< sage exr-product-torus-point >}}
:::

Maps between factors combine into a map between products, and the exercise asks how injectivity and surjectivity
behave under this operation. The answer, that the product map has a property exactly when both factors do, is what
makes coordinates on a product space the product of the coordinates on the factors.

::: {#exr-product-of-maps}
#### Products of maps

For $f : X \to X'$ and $g : Y \to Y'$ define $f \times g : X \times Y \to X' \times Y'$ by $(x, y) \mapsto (f(x),
g(y))$. Show that $f \times g$ is injective exactly when both $f$ and $g$ are, and likewise for surjective.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $f$ and $g$ are injective, $(f(x), g(y)) = (f(x'), g(y'))$ gives $x = x'$ and $y = y'$. If $f$ is not injective,
$f(x) = f(x')$ with $x \neq x'$, then $(x, y)$ and $(x', y)$ have the same image. Surjectivity: every pair $(x', y')$
is hit exactly when every $x'$ and every $y'$ are. The coordinates $(x^\mu, y^m)$ on a product space are the product
of the coordinate maps of the factors (@sec-charts).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The size of the quotient $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ was stated in @exm-quotient-zn, and here it is recorded as a
proposition, first for $n = 3$ and then for every $n$. The proof is division with remainder
(@exr-quotient-general-card), and the three examples that follow unpack what the count says.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-quotient-z3}
#### The quotient $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ has three elements

$\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ has three elements, $\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}$ has five, and $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ has
$n$ elements for every $n \geq 1$.
:::

The three elements of the quotient are the three residue classes, and the example lists them as subsets of the
integers. Each integer lies in exactly one of them, which is the partition property of @def-equivalence-class in
this case.

::: {#exm-z3-elements}
#### The three classes

$[0] = 3\mathbb{Z}$, $[1] = 1 + 3\mathbb{Z}$, $[2] = 2 + 3\mathbb{Z}$: every integer has exactly one remainder.
:::

Both addition and multiplication of integers descend to the three classes, and the example gives the relations that
result. The outcome is the smallest field after $\mathbb{Z}_2$, a first indication that quotients can carry more
structure than the sets they come from.

::: {#exm-z3-table}
#### Addition and multiplication

$1 + 2 = 0$, $2 + 2 = 1$, $2 \cdot 2 = 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}_3$: the operations descend from $\mathbb{Z}$ and make
$\mathbb{Z}_3$ a field, the smallest after $\mathbb{Z}_2$.
:::

The reader is asked to carry out the count for $n = 5$ by hand, following the model of @exm-z3-elements and

as for $n = 3$, every non-zero class has an inverse.

::: {#exr-quotient-z5-card}
#### The five classes of $\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}$

List the classes of $\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}$, show that there are exactly five, and find the multiplicative
inverse of each non-zero class.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The classes are $[r] = r + 5\mathbb{Z}$ for $r = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$: every integer has one of these remainders, and two
distinct remainders differ by less than $5$, so they are not congruent and the five classes are distinct. Since $2
\cdot 3 = 6 \equiv 1$ and $4 \cdot 4 = 16 \equiv 1$, the inverses are $[1]^{-1} = [1]$, $[2]^{-1} = [3]$, $[3]^{-1} =
[2]$ and $[4]^{-1} = [4]$, so $\mathbb{Z}_5$ is a field, like $\mathbb{Z}_3$.
:::

Quotients by different moduli are related when one modulus divides the other, and the exercise explores this for
$12$ and $4$. The map from remainders modulo $12$ to remainders modulo $4$ descends from the identity on the
integers, an instance of the descent criterion of @def-quotient-set with equal-size preimages.

::: {#exr-quotient-z12-classes}
#### Classes modulo 12 and modulo 4

List the classes of $\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}$ that contain multiples of $4$, and explain how $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ maps
onto $\mathbb{Z}_4$.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The multiples of $4$ fall into the classes $[0], [4], [8]$. Since $4 \mid 12$, the remainder modulo $4$ depends only
on the remainder modulo $12$, so $k \mapsto k \bmod 4$ descends to a surjective map $\mathbb{Z}_{12} \to
\mathbb{Z}_4$ whose preimages have three elements each. In Sage:

The last exercise of the section asks for the proof of the count in @prp-quotient-z3: why
congruence modulo $n$ has exactly $n$ classes. Division with remainder provides one representative per class, and
the reader has to show that distinct remainders give distinct classes.

::: {#exr-quotient-general-card}
#### Why $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ has $n$ elements

Prove that congruence modulo $n$ has exactly $n$ classes, using division with remainder.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every integer $a$ is $qn + r$ with a unique remainder $0 \leq r < n$, so $a \sim r$ and every class contains one
of $0, \dots, n - 1$; two distinct remainders differ by less than $n$ and are not congruent, so the $n$ classes
are distinct. This proves @prp-quotient-z3 for every $n \geq 1$.
:::

## Topological spaces {#sec-topology}

To say that two points are close, that a map is continuous or that a set has no edge, one needs to know which
subsets are open. A topology is exactly that: a choice of open sets, subject to three axioms, and every notion of
this section, continuity, homeomorphism, the topology of a subspace or of a quotient, is expressed through open
sets alone. The section starts from the open sets of $\mathbb{R}^n$, abstracts them to the axioms, and then shows how
the circle, the sphere and the rotation group acquire their topologies as subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and as
quotients; a Sage enumeration of all topologies on three points makes the axioms concrete.

### Open sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$

Before a topology can be defined on an abstract set, one needs the example that motivates the axioms: the open sets
of a coordinate space. The picture is a region with no edge, in which every point has some room around it, and the
open ball is the unit of room. Closed sets are then the complements, the regions that contain their edges.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-open-set}
#### Open set in $\mathbb{R}^n$

The **open ball** of radius $\epsilon$ around $p \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is $B_\epsilon(p) = \{x : |x - p| < \epsilon\}$.
A subset $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is **open** if around every one of its points some open ball is contained in
$V$; a subset is **closed** if its complement is open.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the real line, the three kinds of interval illustrate the three possibilities for a set: open, closed, or
neither. The endpoints decide everything, since a ball around an endpoint always sticks out of the interval.

::: {#exm-open-intervals}
#### Intervals

$(0, 2\pi)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}$; $[0, 2\pi]$ is closed and not open, since no ball around $0$ stays inside;
$[0, 2\pi)$ is neither open nor closed.
:::

In the plane the same distinction appears between the open disc, the closed disc and the circle that separates
them. @fig-open-sets shows the room around an interior point and the lack of it at a boundary point; the circle has
no interior points at all in the plane, which is why it is closed and far from open.

::: {#exm-open-disc}
#### Discs

The open disc $\{u^2 + v^2 < 1\}$ is open, the closed disc $\{u^2 + v^2 \leq 1\}$ is closed, and the circle
$\{u^2 + v^2 = 1\}$ is closed (@fig-open-sets): a point on the circle has points off the circle in every ball
around it.
:::

The domains on which coordinates are defined are always open sets, and the example lists the two domains used for
the sphere in this book: an open rectangle of angles and the whole plane. A punctured coordinate space is open too,
a fact used whenever a point has to be removed.

::: {#exm-open-rectangle}
#### Coordinate domains

$(0, \pi) \times (0, 2\pi)$, the domain of spherical coordinates, is open in $\mathbb{R}^2$; so is $\mathbb{R}^2$
itself, the domain of stereographic coordinates; and $\mathbb{R}^n$ minus a point is open. Chart domains
(@sec-charts) are always open sets.
:::

Deciding whether a given set is open or closed is a matter of checking points on its boundary, and the exercise
provides five sets on which to practise. The region above a parabola and the hyperbola are the two-dimensional
cases, and Sage tests the open one numerically by finding a ball around sampled points.

::: {#exr-open-decide}
#### Open, closed or neither

Decide, with a sentence each, whether the following subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{R}^2$ are open, closed, both
or neither: $(1, 2]$, $\mathbb{Z}$, $\{(u, v) : v > u^2\}$, $\{(u, v) : uv = 1\}$, $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(1, 2]$: neither (no ball around $2$ inside, and the complement has no ball around $1$). $\mathbb{Z}$: closed
(its complement is a union of open intervals), not open. $\{v > u^2\}$: open (the region strictly above a parabola;
Sage checks that sampled points have balls inside). $\{uv = 1\}$: closed, a hyperbola. $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus
\{0\}$: open. In Sage, a numerical test of the parabola region:

The definition calls the balls open, and the exercise asks the reader to prove that they deserve the name. The
proof is the triangle inequality and nothing else, and the radius it produces shrinks as the point approaches the
boundary, which explains why boundary points are excluded in @fig-open-sets.

::: {#exr-open-ball-is-open}
#### Open balls are open

Prove that $B_\epsilon(p)$ is an open set: around every $x \in B_\epsilon(p)$ find a ball contained in $B_\epsilon(p)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $x \in B_\epsilon(p)$ and $\delta = \epsilon - |x - p| > 0$. For $y \in B_\delta(x)$ the triangle inequality gives
$|y - p| \leq |y - x| + |x - p| < \delta + |x - p| = \epsilon$, so $B_\delta(x) \subseteq B_\epsilon(p)$. The radius
$\delta$ shrinks as $x$ approaches the boundary, which is why the boundary points themselves are excluded
(@fig-open-sets).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The three properties proved in this exercise, closure under arbitrary unions, closure under finite intersections,
and the failure for infinite intersections, are the properties that the abstract definition of a topology will take
as axioms. The exercise establishes them for the coordinate spaces, so that @def-topological-space has its first
example ready.

::: {#exr-open-union-intersection}
#### Unions and intersections

Show that any union of open sets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is open and any finite intersection is open, and give an infinite
intersection of open sets that is not open.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A point of the union lies in one of the sets, which contains a ball around it, and that ball lies in the union.
A point of a finite intersection has a ball in each set; the smallest radius works for all. Infinitely many: the
intervals $(-1/n, 1/n)$ intersect in $\{0\}$, which is not open. These three facts are the axioms of
@def-topological-space, satisfied by $\mathbb{R}^n$.
:::

### Topological spaces

Only the three properties of @exr-open-union-intersection were ever used in reasoning about open sets, so they can
be taken as axioms on an arbitrary set. The definition does this: a topology is a declaration of which subsets are
open, consistent with unions and finite intersections, and nearness is whatever the declared open sets say it is.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-topological-space}
#### Topological space

A **topology** on a set $X$ is a collection of subsets, the **open sets**, that contains $\emptyset$ and $X$ and
is closed under finite intersections and arbitrary unions. A set with a topology is a **topological space**, an
open set containing $p$ is a **neighbourhood** of $p$, and a subset is **closed** if its complement is open.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example of a topology is the one the axioms were abstracted from. The open sets of @def-open-set satisfy
the axioms by the arguments of @exr-open-union-intersection, and this is the topology meant whenever a coordinate
space appears in this book.

::: {#exm-topology-rn}
#### $\mathbb{R}^n$

The open sets of @def-open-set form a topology on $\mathbb{R}^n$: a union of open sets contains a ball around each
of its points, and so does a finite intersection (take the smallest of the finitely many radii).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-ball-opens-test.sage`.

:::

Every set carries two trivial topologies, the largest and the smallest possible collections of open sets. Between
these extremes there can be many others, and on a three-point set the number is $29$, a count established by
enumeration in @prp-finite-topologies.

::: {#exm-topology-discrete}
#### Discrete and indiscrete topologies

On any set, declaring every subset open gives the **discrete** topology, and declaring only $\emptyset$ and $X$
open gives the **indiscrete** one. On a three-point set there are exactly $29$ topologies between these two
extremes (@prp-finite-topologies).
:::

On a finite set the axioms can be checked by hand, and the example gives one family that passes and one that fails.
The failing family is missing a union, which is the most common way a candidate fails; @exr-finite-topologies
enumerates all the families that pass.

::: {#exm-topology-finite}
#### A topology on three points

On $\{1, 2, 3\}$ the family $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{1, 2\}, \{1, 2, 3\}\}$ is a topology (any union or intersection
of its members is again a member), while $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{1, 2, 3\}\}$ is not, since the union
$\{1, 2\}$ is missing (@exr-finite-topologies).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader is asked to apply the axioms to three more families of subsets of a three-point set. One of them
requires checking both unions and intersections before a verdict is reached, and Sage decides each case by testing
every pair of members.

::: {#exr-topology-axioms-check}
#### Checking the axioms

Decide which of the families $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{2, 3\}, X\}$, $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{1, 2\}, \{1, 3\}, X\}$ and
$\{\emptyset, \{1, 2\}, \{2, 3\}, X\}$ are topologies on $X = \{1, 2, 3\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The first is a topology (unions and intersections of its members stay inside). The second is not: $\{1, 2\} \cap
\{1, 3\} = \{1\}$ is in, but $\{1, 2\} \cup \{1, 3\} = X$ is in too, so check again: all unions and intersections
are present, it is a topology. The third is not: $\{1, 2\} \cap \{2, 3\} = \{2\}$ is missing. Sage decides each case
by testing the axioms:

{{< sage exr-topology-axioms-check >}}
:::

On a two-element set there are only sixteen families of subsets, and the exercise asks which of them are
topologies. The two asymmetric answers, the Sierpiński topologies, are the smallest examples of a space in which
the points are not interchangeable, and they return in @exr-hausdorff-sierpinski.

#### Topologies on two points

List all topologies on $\{1, 2\}$.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}

X\}$ and $\{\emptyset, \{2\}, X\}$. In Sage, by enumerating the $2^4 = 16$ families:

Two topologies on the same set can be combined, and the exercise asks what happens under intersection and under
union. The intersection always works, the union usually does not, and the counterexample on three points shows
which axiom is lost.

::: {#exr-topology-intersection}
#### The intersection of two topologies

Show that the common open sets of two topologies on $X$ form a topology, and that their union need not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A union or finite intersection of sets open in both topologies is open in both, and $\emptyset$, $X$ are in
both, so the intersection is a topology. The union of the two Sierpiński topologies on $\{1, 2\}$ is $\{\emptyset,
\{1\}, \{2\}, X\}$, which is a topology, but on three points the union of $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, X\}$ and $\{\emptyset,
\{2\}, X\}$ lacks $\{1, 2\}$ and is not.
:::

The circle, the sphere and the rotation group sit inside coordinate spaces, and they should inherit a topology from
there. The next definition says how: the open sets of a subset are the traces of the open sets of the ambient
space, and the picture is a region of the plane cutting an arc out of the circle.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-subspace-topology}
#### Subspace topology

A subset $Y \subseteq X$ of a topological space inherits the **subspace topology**: its open sets are the
intersections $U \cap Y$ with $U$ open in $X$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The circle inherits its topology from the plane, and the example describes what the inherited open sets look like:
arcs and unions of arcs. @fig-open-sets shows one such arc as the trace of an open disc, which is the picture to
keep for every subspace.

::: {#exm-subspace-circle}
#### The circle

The circle $S^1 \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ carries the subspace topology: an open set of the circle is the intersection of
the circle with an open set of the plane, an open arc or a union of arcs (@fig-open-sets).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

:::

The sphere inside three-dimensional space and the rotation group inside the nine-dimensional space of matrices
acquire their topologies in the same way. An open set of rotations is a set of matrices whose entries vary within
open ranges, and this is the sense in which two rotations can be close to each other.

::: {#exm-subspace-sphere}
#### The sphere and the rotation group

The sphere $S^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ and the rotation group $SO(3) \subset \mathbb{R}^{9}$ (as $3 \times 3$ matrices)
are subspaces; an open set of the sphere is a cap or a union of caps, and an open set of $SO(3)$ is a set of
rotations whose matrix entries vary within open ranges.
:::

The subspace topology can declare open a set that is not open in the ambient space, and a half-open interval shows
how. The example makes the point that openness is always relative to the space one is in, a point that
@exr-subspace-open develops on the circle.

::: {#exm-subspace-interval}
#### Intervals

$[0, 1) \subset \mathbb{R}$ as a subspace has $[0, \tfrac12) = (-\tfrac12, \tfrac12) \cap [0, 1)$ among its open sets,
although $[0, \tfrac12)$ is not open in $\mathbb{R}$: openness is relative to the space.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader is asked to decide which halves of the circle are open in the circle's own topology. The open upper half
is the trace of an open half-plane, while the closed upper half contains two points at which every arc sticks out,
so the answer hinges on the two points on the horizontal axis.

::: {#exr-subspace-open}
#### Open sets of a subspace

Show that the upper half of the circle, $\{(X, Y) \in S^1 : Y > 0\}$, is open in the circle, and that the closed
upper half $\{Y \geq 0\}$ is not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The open upper half-plane $\{Y > 0\}$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and its intersection with the circle is the open
upper half, which is therefore open in the subspace topology. The closed upper half contains the points $(\pm 1,
0)$, and every arc around them contains points with $Y < 0$, so no open set of the plane cuts out exactly the
closed half.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

Some subsets of the line inherit the discrete topology, in which every point is isolated, and the exercise
identifies two of them. Adding the limit point $0$ to the sequence $1/n$ destroys discreteness, which shows how a
single point can change the inherited topology.

::: {#exr-subspace-discrete}
#### Discrete subspaces

Show that $\mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{R}$ and $\{1/n : n \geq 1\} \subset \mathbb{R}$ carry the discrete topology as
subspaces, and that $\{0\} \cup \{1/n\}$ does not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\{k\} = (k - \tfrac12, k + \tfrac12) \cap \mathbb{Z}$ is open in $\mathbb{Z}$, so every subset is open. Likewise
$\{1/n\}$ is cut out by a small interval around $1/n$ not containing its neighbours. With $0$ added, every open
set of $\mathbb{R}$ containing $0$ contains infinitely many $1/n$, so $\{0\}$ is not open in the subspace: the
subspace is not discrete.
:::
