A subset of a subset can inherit its topology in two ways, directly from the ambient space or in two steps, and the
exercise shows that the two agree. The consequence is that the topology of an arc of the circle does not depend on
whether the arc is regarded inside the circle or inside the plane.

::: {#exr-subspace-transitive}
#### Subspace of a subspace

For $Z \subseteq Y \subseteq X$, show that the subspace topology $Z$ inherits from $Y$ equals the one it inherits
from $X$ directly.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
An open set of $Z$ from $Y$ is $(U \cap Y) \cap Z$ with $U$ open in $X$, and $(U \cap Y) \cap Z = U \cap Z$ since
$Z \subseteq Y$, which is an open set of $Z$ from $X$; conversely every $U \cap Z$ has this form. So the topology of
an arc of the circle is the same whether the arc is viewed inside the circle or inside the plane.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

With open sets available on both sides, a map between topological spaces can be called continuous without any
mention of distances. The definition asks that open sets pull back to open sets, and the picture is that points
close to a given point are sent close to its image; for subsets of coordinate spaces this is the familiar
$\epsilon$-$\delta$ condition.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-continuous-map}
#### Continuous map

A map $f : X \to Y$ between topological spaces is **continuous** if the preimage $f^{-1}(V)$ of every open set
$V \subseteq Y$ is open in $X$. For maps between subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ this is the $\epsilon$-$\delta$
definition: points close to $p$ are sent close to $f(p)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-eps-delta-test.sage`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Sets.Continuous.continuous_iff_eps_delta >}}

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The elementary functions are continuous, and the example contrasts them with a step function, which is not. The
failure is witnessed by one open interval whose preimage contains an endpoint without any room around it, the
computation that @exr-preimages asks for in full.

::: {#exm-continuous-elementary}
#### Elementary functions and a step

$\cos$, $\sin$, $\exp$, polynomials and their compositions are continuous on $\mathbb{R}$; the step function
$x \mapsto 0$ for $x < 0$, $1$ for $x \geq 0$ is not: the preimage of the open set $(\tfrac12, 2)$ is $[0, \infty)$,
not open (@exr-preimages).
:::

The parametrisations of the circle and the sphere are continuous because their components are, a principle that
reduces continuity into a coordinate space to the continuity of finitely many real functions. These maps are the
inverses of charts, and their continuity is half of what makes a chart a homeomorphism.

::: {#exm-continuous-chart}
#### Parametrisations

$\varphi \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ is continuous from $\mathbb{R}$ to the circle, and so is $(\theta,
\varphi) \mapsto (\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \sin\theta\sin\varphi, \cos\theta)$ from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to the sphere, as
their components are continuous functions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

:::

Operations on matrices are continuous because each entry of the result is a polynomial in the entries of the
inputs. The orbit map on the rotation group is of this type, and its continuity is the ingredient that
@exr-continuous-composition and @exr-sphere-quotient-homeomorphism use.

::: {#exm-continuous-matrix}
#### Matrix maps

Matrix multiplication, the determinant and the orbit map $g \mapsto g \cdot (0, 0, 1)$ on $SO(3)$ are continuous,
since each entry of the result is a polynomial in the entries of the arguments.
:::

Rounding down to the nearest integer gives a function with infinitely many discontinuities, and the exercise asks
the reader to locate all of them by the preimage criterion. A single well-chosen open interval around each integer
value does the job, and the same interval shows continuity between consecutive integers.

::: {#exr-continuous-floor}
#### The floor function

Find all points where $x \mapsto \lfloor x\rfloor$ is discontinuous, by exhibiting an open set whose preimage is not
open.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The preimage of the open interval $(k - \tfrac12, k + \tfrac12)$ is $[k, k + 1)$, not open at $k$: the floor
function is discontinuous at every integer and continuous elsewhere (on $(k, k + 1)$ it is constant). Sage
samples the jumps:

Composition of continuous maps is continuous, and the proof is one line about preimages. The exercise asks for that
line and for its application to a point carried along by a continuous family of rotations, which produces a
continuous curve on the sphere; curves of this kind are the geodesics of the sphere.

::: {#exr-continuous-composition}
#### Compositions and the orbit map

Prove that the composition of continuous maps is continuous, and conclude that $t \mapsto R(t) \cdot (0, 0, 1)$,
for a continuous family of rotations $R(t)$, is a continuous curve on the sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(g \circ f)^{-1}(W) = f^{-1}(g^{-1}(W))$: an open $W$ has open $g^{-1}(W)$, whose preimage under $f$ is open. The
curve is the composition of $t \mapsto R(t)$, continuous into the matrices, with the orbit map, continuous by
@exm-continuous-matrix. Paths on a sphere obtained by rotating a point are the geodesics of @sec-geodesics.
:::

When two spaces are related by a bijection that is continuous in both directions, their open sets correspond
exactly and nothing topological distinguishes them. The next definition names such a bijection, and the picture is
a deformation without tearing or gluing; @exr-homeomorphism-invariance makes the correspondence of open sets
precise.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-homeomorphism}
#### Homeomorphism

A **homeomorphism** is a continuous bijection whose inverse is also continuous; two spaces related by one are
**homeomorphic**, indistinguishable as topological spaces.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The tangent, already a bijection in @exm-bijection-cube, is continuous with continuous inverse, so an open interval
and the whole line are the same space topologically. The example also announces that a closed interval is a
different space, a distinction that needs compactness to prove.

::: {#exm-homeomorphism-interval}
#### Intervals and the line

$x \mapsto \tan x$ is a homeomorphism from $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$ onto $\mathbb{R}$: an open interval and the whole
line are homeomorphic. A closed interval is not homeomorphic to an open one (@sec-compact-connected explains why).
:::

Stereographic projection is a homeomorphism from the punctured sphere onto the plane, which is why it serves as a
chart. The example also exhibits a continuous bijection that is not a homeomorphism, the wrapping of a half-open
interval onto the circle, whose inverse jumps at one point; continuity of the inverse is a genuine extra condition.

::: {#exm-homeomorphism-sphere}
#### The sphere minus a point

Stereographic projection (@sec-charts) is a homeomorphism from the sphere minus the north pole onto the plane
$\mathbb{R}^2$; a continuous bijection whose inverse is not continuous is $\varphi \mapsto (\cos\varphi,
\sin\varphi)$ from $[0, 2\pi)$ onto the circle, whose inverse jumps at $(1, 0)$.
:::

Radial projection shows that the boundary of a square and the circle are homeomorphic, as any picture of a square
being rounded off suggests. Showing that two spaces are not homeomorphic needs an invariant, and the example
introduces the standard one: count the pieces left after removing a point.

::: {#exm-homeomorphism-square}
#### Square and circle

The boundary of a square is homeomorphic to the circle by radial projection $x \mapsto x/|x|$; a figure eight is
not homeomorphic to the circle, since removing its crossing point leaves two pieces while removing a point from a
circle leaves one (@sec-compact-connected).
:::

The reader is asked to verify the homeomorphism of @exm-homeomorphism-interval in detail and to find a second one,
from the interval $(-1, 1)$ onto the line. In both cases a strictly increasing continuous function with the right
limits at the ends is a homeomorphism, and Sage checks the compositions and the derivative.

::: {#exr-homeomorphism-tan}
#### $\tan$ and its inverse

Verify that $\tan : (-\pi/2, \pi/2) \to \mathbb{R}$ and $\arctan$ are inverse continuous bijections, and that
$x \mapsto x/(1 - x^2)$ is a homeomorphism from $(-1, 1)$ onto $\mathbb{R}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tan$ is continuous, strictly increasing and unbounded in both directions on $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$, hence a bijection
onto $\mathbb{R}$, with the continuous inverse $\arctan$. The second map is continuous, strictly increasing
(derivative $(1 + x^2)/(1 - x^2)^2 > 0$) and tends to $\pm\infty$ at $\pm1$, hence a homeomorphism. Sage checks
the compositions and the derivative:

{{< sage exr-homeomorphism-tan >}}
:::

The point-removal invariant of @exm-homeomorphism-square is applied here to two intervals that differ by a single
endpoint. Removing that endpoint leaves one piece in one interval and two in the other, and the exercise asks for
the argument that this contradicts the existence of a homeomorphism.

::: {#exr-homeomorphism-half-open}
#### $[0, 1)$ and $(0, 1)$ are not homeomorphic

Prove it by removing a point.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A homeomorphism $f : [0, 1) \to (0, 1)$ would restrict to a homeomorphism from $[0, 1) \setminus \{0\} = (0, 1)$
onto $(0, 1) \setminus \{f(0)\}$. The first space is connected (@def-connected), the second is the union of the
two disjoint open intervals $(0, f(0))$ and $(f(0), 1)$, not connected, and connectedness is preserved by
homeomorphisms. Removing points is the standard way to distinguish spaces (@exm-homeomorphism-square).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

:::

A homeomorphism sends open sets to open sets, not only preimages of open sets to open sets, and the exercise asks
for the short proof. This is the statement that makes "indistinguishable as topological spaces" literally true: the
two topologies correspond under the bijection.

::: {#exr-homeomorphism-invariance}
#### Homeomorphisms preserve open sets

Show that a homeomorphism $f : X \to Y$ sends open sets to open sets and closed sets to closed sets.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $U$ open in $X$, $f(U) = (f^{-1})^{-1}(U)$ is the preimage of $U$ under the continuous map $f^{-1}$, hence
open; closed sets are complements of open sets and $f$ is a bijection. Thus a homeomorphism identifies the two
topologies completely, which is what "indistinguishable as topological spaces" means.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.**

The quotient sets of @sec-relations-products become topological spaces by the next definition, which declares a set
of classes open when the elements it collects form an open set. The picture is the circle inheriting its arcs from
the periodic open sets of the line, and the criterion for continuity of a map out of the quotient is the
topological version of descent.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-quotient-topology}
#### Quotient topology

A quotient set $X/{\sim}$ (@def-quotient-set) of a topological space carries the **quotient topology**: a set of
classes is open if its preimage under the quotient map is open in $X$. A map from $X/{\sim}$ is then continuous
exactly when its composition with the quotient map is continuous.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-quotient-continuous-test.sage`.

:::

\sin\varphi)$: the map is a continuous bijection, and the image of an open interval of angles is an open arc, so

The bijection of @exm-quotient-sphere between the quotient of the rotation group and the sphere is likewise a
homeomorphism. This is the topological meaning of the sphere as a coset space of the rotation group, and
@exr-sphere-quotient-homeomorphism in the final section supplies the proof, which needs compactness.

::: {#exm-quotient-sphere-top}
#### $SO(3)/SO(2)$

The quotient of $SO(3)$ by the relation "same image of the north pole" is homeomorphic to the sphere by
$[g] \mapsto g \cdot (0, 0, 1)$; this is what "the sphere is the coset space $SO(3)/SO(2)$" means topologically
(@sec-coset-spaces).

Gluing the opposite edges of a square, the construction of @exr-quotient-square, produces a space homeomorphic to
the torus as a product of two circles. The homeomorphism is the pair of wrapping maps, one for each coordinate, so
the torus can be studied either as a quotient or as a product.

Identifying opposite edges of the square $[0, 2\pi] \times [0, 2\pi]$, $(0, v) \sim (2\pi, v)$ and $(u, 0) \sim
(u, 2\pi)$, gives a quotient homeomorphic to the torus $S^1 \times S^1$, by $(u, v) \mapsto ((\cos u, \sin u),
(\cos v, \sin v))$.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader is asked to build the circle from a closed interval by identifying its two endpoints and to prove that
the result is homeomorphic to the circle. The contrast with the half-open interval, where the same map fails to be
a homeomorphism, shows that the identification is what repairs the continuity of the inverse.

::: {#exr-quotient-interval-circle}
#### The circle from an interval

Show that $[0, 2\pi]$ with $0 \sim 2\pi$ is homeomorphic to the circle, and explain why $[0, 2\pi)$ with no
identification is not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[\varphi] \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ is a continuous bijection from the quotient onto the circle; an
open set of the quotient containing $[0]$ has preimage containing $[0, \epsilon) \cup (2\pi - \epsilon, 2\pi]$,
whose image is an open arc around $(1, 0)$, so the inverse is continuous. On $[0, 2\pi)$ the same map is a
continuous bijection but $[0, \epsilon)$ is open while its image, a half-open arc, is not open in the circle.
:::

The exercise asks for a description of which sets of classes are open in the quotient of the line by full turns, in
terms of periodic open subsets of the line. It then shows that the quotient map is open, sending open sets to open
sets, a property not shared by all continuous maps, and Sage checks the periodicity on a sample.

::: {#exr-quotient-open-sets}
#### Open sets of the quotient

Describe the open sets of $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ in terms of open sets of $\mathbb{R}$, and show that the
quotient map sends open sets to open sets.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A set of classes is open when its preimage, a union of classes, is open in $\mathbb{R}$: the $2\pi$-periodic open
sets. For $U$ open in $\mathbb{R}$, the preimage of $\pi(U)$ is $\bigcup_k(U + 2\pi k)$, a union of open sets,
so $\pi(U)$ is open. Sage checks periodicity of a sampled open set:

{{< sage exr-quotient-open-sets >}}
:::

Gluing the edges of a square with a half twist instead of straight produces a different surface, and the exercise
asks the reader to describe it and its boundary. The comparison with the cylinder, obtained from the same square by
a different relation, is the first encounter with a twisted bundle, a theme of the bundle chapters.

::: {#exr-quotient-moebius}
#### The Möbius band

Identify the edges $(0, v) \sim (1, 1 - v)$ of the square $[0, 1]^2$. Describe the quotient, its boundary, and
compare with the cylinder obtained from $(0, v) \sim (1, v)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The quotient is the Möbius band: the two vertical edges are glued with a half twist. The boundary is a single
circle (follow the top edge, then, after the twist, the bottom edge), whereas the cylinder has two boundary
circles. Both are quotients of the same square by different equivalence relations, and both are the total spaces
of bundles over the circle (@sec-bundles), the cylinder trivial and the Möbius band not.
:::

The topologies on a set are ordered by inclusion of their collections of open sets, from indiscrete to discrete.
The example explains how this order affects continuity: more open sets on the domain make continuity easier, more
on the codomain make it harder.

::: {#exm-topologies-lattice}
#### Finer and coarser

The $29$ topologies are ordered by inclusion, from the indiscrete (coarsest) to the discrete (finest): a topology
with more open sets makes more maps out of the space continuous and fewer maps into it.
:::

## Compact and connected spaces {#sec-compact-connected}

Three global properties of a topological space decide much of what can be done on it. A Hausdorff space is one in
which points can be told apart by open sets, so that limits are unique; a compact space is one on which every
continuous function is bounded and attains its extremes, and on which the eigenvalues of a Laplacian form a
discrete set; a connected space is one in one piece. The section defines the three properties, with intervals,
spheres, rotation groups and finite graphs as examples, and ends with the enumeration of the Hausdorff topologies
on three points.

### Hausdorff spaces

The first of the three global properties concerns whether open sets can distinguish points. The picture is two
points each sitting in its own open set, with the two sets not overlapping, and the consequences listed in the
definition, unique limits and closed points, are what make this property a requirement for manifolds.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-hausdorff}
#### Hausdorff space

A topological space is **Hausdorff** if any two distinct points have disjoint neighbourhoods. In a Hausdorff
space limits are unique and single points are closed sets; manifolds (@sec-manifolds) are required to be
Hausdorff.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Sets.Hausdorff.hausdorff_consequences >}}

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Coordinate spaces are Hausdorff because two distinct points are at a positive distance, and half that distance
gives the disjoint balls. Since the property passes to subspaces, all the geometric examples of this chapter,
circle, sphere, torus and rotation group, are Hausdorff at once.

::: {#exm-hausdorff-rn}
#### $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its subspaces

Two distinct points of $\mathbb{R}^n$ at distance $d$ have disjoint balls of radius $d/2$; every subspace of a
Hausdorff space is Hausdorff, so the circle, the sphere, the torus and $SO(3)$ all are.
:::

Quotients can destroy the Hausdorff property even when the original space has it, and the example gives the
standard case, the line modulo rational differences, where every class is dense. Quotients of a group by a closed
subgroup escape this, which is why coset spaces are formed with closed subgroups.

::: {#exm-hausdorff-quotient}
#### Quotients can fail

The quotient of $\mathbb{R}$ by $x \sim y$ iff $x - y \in \mathbb{Q}$ is not Hausdorff: every open set of the
quotient is empty or everything, because every open interval contains a member of every class. Quotients of a group
by a closed subgroup, such as $SO(3)/SO(2)$, are Hausdorff, which is one reason the subgroup $R$ in a coset space
$S/R$ is taken closed (@sec-coset-spaces).
:::

The claim in @def-hausdorff that a single point forms a closed set is proved here. The proof assembles the
complement of the point from the neighbourhoods separating it from every other point, and the exercise also notes
that the converse fails.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-points-closed}
#### Points are closed

Prove that in a Hausdorff space every single point $\{p\}$ is a closed set.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For each $q \neq p$ choose disjoint neighbourhoods $U_q \ni q$, $V_q \ni p$; then $U_q$ misses $p$. The union of
all $U_q$ is open and equals $X \setminus \{p\}$, so $\{p\}$ is closed. The converse fails: the cofinite topology
on an infinite set has closed points but is not Hausdorff.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

Doubling the origin of the real line gives the standard example of a space that looks like the line near every
point and yet is not Hausdorff. The exercise asks for the proof that the two origins cannot be separated, and this
example is the reason the definition of a manifold imposes the Hausdorff property as a separate condition.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-two-origins}
#### The line with two origins

Take two copies of $\mathbb{R}$ and identify $x \sim x'$ for all $x \neq 0$. Show the quotient is not Hausdorff.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The two origins $0$ and $0'$ are distinct points of the quotient; a neighbourhood of either contains the image of
an interval $(-\epsilon, \epsilon)$ minus the origin, so any two neighbourhoods meet. The space is locally like
$\mathbb{R}$ everywhere but is not a manifold: this is why @def-manifold requires the Hausdorff property
separately.
:::

### Compact spaces

The second global property replaces finiteness for infinite spaces: whatever can be done with finitely many open
sets can be done on the whole space. The definition phrases this through open covers, and the picture for subsets
of a coordinate space is a closed and bounded set, with the consequence that continuous functions on it attain
their extremes.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-compact}
#### Compact space

An **open cover** of a space is a family of open sets whose union is the whole space. The space is **compact** if
every open cover has a finite subfamily that still covers. For subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ this is equivalent to being
closed and bounded (the Heine-Borel theorem), and a continuous real function on a compact space is bounded and
attains its maximum and minimum.
:::

The circle, the sphere, the torus and the rotation group are closed and bounded in their coordinate spaces, so they
are compact, and so is every coset space of a compact group. The example also states the consequence that matters
most for this book: on a compact space the Laplacian has a discrete spectrum, the origin of the Kaluza-Klein
towers.

::: {#exm-compact-spheres}
#### Spheres, tori, groups

$S^1$, $S^2$, $T^2$ and $SO(3)$ are closed and bounded in their ambient spaces, hence compact; so is every coset
space $S/R$ of a compact group $S$. On a compact space the eigenvalues of the Laplacian form a discrete set, which
is why the spectra of @sec-kk-tower are towers.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader is asked to prove the non-compactness of the open interval claimed in @exm-compact-interval by
exhibiting an open cover none of whose finite subfamilies suffices. The second part asks why the same cover does
not work for the closed interval, and the answer is the Heine-Borel mechanism in miniature.

::: {#exr-compact-proof}
#### A cover without a finite subcover

Show that the open interval $(0, 1)$ is not compact by exhibiting an open cover with no finite subcover, and
explain why the same cover cannot be used for $[0, 1]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The sets $U_n = (1/n, 1)$, $n \geq 2$, cover $(0, 1)$, but any finite subfamily is contained in $(1/N, 1)$ for its
largest $N$ and misses $(0, 1/N]$. For $[0, 1]$ the family does not cover the points $0$ and $1$; open sets
containing them contain $(-\epsilon, \epsilon)$ and $(1 - \epsilon, 1 + \epsilon)$, and together with finitely many
$U_n$ they cover $[0, 1]$, which is the Heine-Borel conclusion.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

Compactness guarantees that a continuous function attains its maximum and minimum, and the exercise shows the
guarantee in action and its failure without compactness. The same function on a closed and on an open interval has
the same maximum but loses its minimum when the endpoint is removed, and Sage computes the critical points.

::: {#exr-compact-extremes}
#### Extremes on a compact set

Find the maximum and minimum of $f(x) = xe^{-x}$ on $[0, 2]$, and explain why $f$ has a maximum but no minimum
on the open interval $(0, 2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f'(x) = (1 - x)e^{-x}$ vanishes at $x = 1$, the maximum $e^{-1}$, attained inside $(0, 2)$ as well; the minimum
on $[0, 2]$ is $f(0) = 0$ at the endpoint, which $(0, 2)$ lacks: on the open interval $f > 0$ with infimum $0$ not
attained. Compactness guarantees attained extremes; without it they may be missing. In Sage:

{{< sage exr-compact-extremes >}}
:::

A closed subset of a compact space is itself compact, and the exercise asks for the proof, which adds the
complement of the subset to any cover. The consequence is a second proof that the circle and the spheres are
compact, as closed subsets of closed discs and balls.

::: {#exr-compact-closed-subset}
#### Closed subsets of compact spaces

Prove that a closed subset of a compact space is compact, and deduce that the circle $\{u^2 + v^2 = 1\}$ is
compact from the compactness of the closed disc.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Given an open cover of the closed subset $C$, add the open set $X \setminus C$ to get a cover of $X$; a finite
subcover of $X$, with $X \setminus C$ removed, is a finite subcover of $C$. The circle is closed in the compact
disc $[-1, 1]^2 \cap \{u^2 + v^2 \leq 1\}$, so it is compact; the same argument gives the compactness of every
sphere, as a closed subset of a closed ball.
:::

### Connected spaces

The third global property asks whether a space is in one piece. The definition phrases this negatively, through the
impossibility of splitting the space into two disjoint non-empty open sets, and the picture is of a set that cannot
be pulled apart; the components of the definition are the pieces when it can.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-connected}
#### Connected space

A space is **connected** if it is not the union of two disjoint non-empty open sets. Its maximal connected
subsets are its **connected components**, and they partition the space.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-components-partition-test.sage`.

**Lean.**

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The circle, the sphere, the torus and the coordinate spaces are connected, and the example shows how the circle
behaves under removal of points: one removal leaves it connected, two removals cut it into two arcs. This behaviour
is the invariant used in @exm-homeomorphism-square, and @fig-components-graph shows a finite model of it.

::: {#exm-connected-circle}
#### Circles and spheres

$S^1$, $S^2$, $T^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$ are connected. Removing one point from a circle leaves it connected; removing
two points disconnects it into two arcs, the two open arcs between them (@fig-components-graph).
:::

The group of all orthogonal transformations of space has two pieces, the rotations and the reflections, separated
by the sign of the determinant. The example makes the point that a continuous function taking only two values
splits a space, and it explains why the Lie algebra of a group sees only the component of the identity.

::: {#exm-connected-groups}
#### Groups with two components

$O(3)$, the rotations and reflections of space, has two connected components, the rotations $SO(3)$ (determinant
$+1$) and the reflections (determinant $-1$), since the determinant is continuous and takes only the values $\pm 1$.
A Lie algebra (@sec-lie-algebras) sees only the component of the identity.
:::

:::

A finite graph is a discrete model of a space, and connectedness of the graph is the combinatorial version of
connectedness of the space. The example introduces the graph with two components and the six-cycle of
@fig-components-graph, which behaves like the circle under removal of vertices.

::: {#exm-connected-finite}
#### Finite models

A finite graph is a finite model of a space, its vertices the regions and its edges the adjacencies: the graph of
@fig-components-graph with edges $AB$, $BC$, $DE$ has two components, and the six-cycle, a discrete circle,
behaves like the circle under the removal of one or two vertices (@exr-connected-components).
:::

The determinant argument of @exm-connected-groups is applied here to the invertible two-by-two matrices and to the
orthogonal group of the plane. The exercise asks for at least two components in the first case and exactly two in
the second, where each component is a circle, and Sage exhibits a path within one of them.

::: {#exr-connected-gl2}
#### The invertible matrices

Show that the set $GL(2, \mathbb{R})$ of invertible $2 \times 2$ real matrices has at least two connected
components, and that $O(2)$ has exactly two.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The determinant is continuous and never zero on $GL(2, \mathbb{R})$, so $\{\det > 0\}$ and $\{\det < 0\}$ are
disjoint non-empty open sets covering it: at least two components (in fact exactly two). $O(2)$ consists of the
rotations (a circle, connected) and the reflections (another circle), with $\det = \pm1$: exactly two components.
Sage finds a path of rotations and the sign of the determinant:

{{< sage exr-connected-gl2 >}}
:::

Continuous maps preserve connectedness, and the exercise asks for the proof by pulling back a splitting of the
image to a splitting of the domain. The intermediate value theorem is the corollary when the domain is an interval,
and the result is used again in @exr-path-connected-implies.

::: {#exr-connected-image}
#### Continuous images of connected spaces

Prove that the image of a connected space under a continuous map is connected, and deduce the intermediate value
theorem for a continuous $f : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $f(X) = U \cup V$ with $U$, $V$ disjoint non-empty open sets of $f(X)$, then $f^{-1}(U)$ and $f^{-1}(V)$ are
disjoint non-empty open sets covering $X$, contradicting connectedness. A connected subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is an
interval, so $f([0, 1])$ is an interval containing $f(0)$ and $f(1)$, hence every value between them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

A more concrete way for a space to be in one piece is that any two of its points can be joined by a continuous
curve. The next definition introduces paths and the spaces in which every pair of points is joined by one, and
records that this stronger property implies connectedness, which @exr-path-connected-implies asks the reader to
prove.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-path-connected}
#### Path-connected space

A **path** from $p$ to $q$ is a continuous map $\gamma : [0, 1] \to X$ with $\gamma(0) = p$ and $\gamma(1) = q$.
A space is **path-connected** if any two of its points are joined by a path; a path-connected space is connected.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the sphere the natural path between two points runs along a great circle, and in a coordinate space along a
straight segment. Both spaces are therefore path-connected, and the explicit formulas for such paths are what the
exercises ask for.

::: {#exm-path-sphere}
#### Spheres

Any two points of $S^2$ are joined by an arc of a great circle, and any two points of $\mathbb{R}^n$ by a straight
segment $\gamma(t) = (1 - t)p + tq$; both spaces are path-connected.
:::

The rotation group is path-connected, and the example gives the path: turn gradually about the axis of the given
rotation until the full angle is reached. No path leads from a rotation to a reflection, because the determinant
cannot jump, which is the two-component structure of @exm-connected-groups seen through paths.

::: {#exm-path-rotations}
#### Rotations

Any rotation is joined to the identity by the path $t \mapsto R(t\alpha)$ of rotations about the same axis by the
angles $t\alpha$, so $SO(3)$ is path-connected; no path joins a rotation to a reflection, as the determinant would
have to jump from $1$ to $-1$.
:::

The reader is asked to write down an explicit path along a great circle from the north pole to a point on the
equator and to check that it stays on the sphere. The check is the Pythagorean identity, and the solution also
evaluates it symbolically in Sage.

::: {#exr-path-great-circle}
#### A path on the sphere

Write down a path on $S^2$ from the north pole to the point $(1, 0, 0)$ along a great circle, and check that it
stays on the sphere.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\gamma(t) = (\sin\tfrac{\pi t}{2}, 0, \cos\tfrac{\pi t}{2})$, a quarter of the great circle through the pole in the
$XZ$-plane: $|\gamma(t)|^2 = \sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$. In Sage:

{{< sage exr-path-great-circle >}}

The path of @exm-path-rotations joins a rotation to the identity, and the exercise asks for a path between two
arbitrary rotations. The construction composes a path from the identity with a fixed rotation, and it relies on the
fact that every rotation has an axis, which is the surjectivity of the exponential map for this group.

::: {#exr-path-rotations-connect}
#### Connecting two rotations

Given rotations $R_1$ and $R_2$, construct a path in $SO(3)$ from $R_1$ to $R_2$, using the fact that every
rotation is a rotation about some axis by some angle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$R_1^{-1}R_2$ is a rotation by some angle $\alpha$ about some axis $n$; let $R(t)$ be the rotation by $t\alpha$ about
$n$, a continuous path from the identity to $R_1^{-1}R_2$. Then $t \mapsto R_1R(t)$ is a path from $R_1$ to $R_2$.
The existence of the axis is the statement that $SO(3)$ is the image of the exponential map of @sec-exponential.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The implication stated in @def-path-connected is proved here using the preservation of connectedness under
continuous maps from @exr-connected-image. The exercise also records that the converse fails, with the topologist's
sine curve as the standard counterexample.

::: {#exr-path-connected-implies}
#### Path-connected implies connected

Prove that a path-connected space is connected, using @exr-connected-image.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Suppose $X = U \cup V$ with $U$, $V$ disjoint non-empty open sets; pick $p \in U$, $q \in V$ and a path $\gamma$
from $p$ to $q$. Its image $\gamma([0, 1])$ is connected (image of the connected interval), yet it is covered by
the disjoint non-empty open sets $U \cap \gamma([0, 1])$ and $V \cap \gamma([0, 1])$: a contradiction. The converse
fails for the topologist's sine curve, the closure of the graph of $\sin(1/x)$, which is connected but not
path-connected.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.**

Finiteness is what makes the Hausdorff topology unique, and the example shows that on an infinite set there are
many, including the usual and the discrete topologies on the line. The contrast explains why the enumeration
results of this chapter are statements about finite sets only.

::: {#exm-hausdorff-infinite}
#### Infinite spaces

On an infinite set there are many Hausdorff topologies, for instance the usual one on $\mathbb{R}$ and the discrete
one, which differ; finiteness is what collapses the count to one.
:::

::: {#exr-hausdorff-finite}
#### Which finite topologies are Hausdorff?

Explain why the only Hausdorff topology on a finite set is the discrete one, and compare with the count of
@exr-finite-topologies.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In a Hausdorff space every point is closed, so in a finite space every subset, a finite union of points, is
closed, hence every subset is open: the topology is discrete. The enumeration of @exr-finite-topologies finds
exactly one Hausdorff topology among the $29$, the discrete one, in agreement.
:::

**Lean.**

A weaker separation condition than Hausdorff asks only that every point be closed, and the exercise counts the
three-point topologies satisfying it. On a finite set the two conditions turn out to agree, and the solution
tests in Sage which topologies contain the complement of each point.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-count-t1}
#### Topologies with closed points

Count the topologies on three points in which every single point is closed, and compare with the Hausdorff count.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Exactly one again, the discrete topology: if all points are closed in a finite space, all subsets are closed, hence
open. In Sage, testing which of the $29$ topologies contain the complement of each point:

{{< sage exr-hausdorff-count-t1 >}}

**Sage.** `set-t1-three-test.sage` instances `(F = Finset.univ)`, `(F = {∅, Finset.univ})`, `(F = {∅, {0}, {0, 1}, Finset.univ})`.

The two-point topology with a single open singleton is the smallest in which separation fails, and the exercise
asks for an inventory of its neighbourhoods, its limits and its closed points. Non-unique limits and a non-closed
point appear together, as @def-hausdorff predicts they should in a non-Hausdorff space.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-sierpinski}
#### The Sierpiński space

For the topology $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{1, 2\}\}$ on $\{1, 2\}$, list the neighbourhoods of each point, decide
whether limits are unique, and which points are closed.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Neighbourhoods of $1$: $\{1\}$ and $\{1, 2\}$; of $2$: only $\{1, 2\}$. The constant sequence $1, 1, 1, \dots$
converges to $1$ and also to $2$, since every neighbourhood of $2$ contains $1$: limits are not unique. The point
$2$ is closed ($\{1\}$ is open), the point $1$ is not. One of the four two-point topologies, and not Hausdorff.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

## Exercises {#sec-sets-topology-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Three exercises combining the sections of this chapter.

The first shows that a quotient of a non-compact space can be compact, by using the compactness of a closed
interval and the continuity of the quotient map. It also asks for the Hausdorff property of the quotient circle,
which has to be checked because quotients can lose it, as @exm-hausdorff-quotient showed.

::: {#exr-circle-quotient-compact}
#### The circle as a compact quotient of a non-compact space

Show that $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ with the quotient topology is compact and Hausdorff although $\mathbb{R}$ is
not compact.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The quotient map restricted to the compact interval $[0, 2\pi]$ is still surjective and continuous, and a
continuous image of a compact space is compact (a cover of the image pulls back to a cover of the interval with a
finite subcover). Hausdorff: two distinct classes have representatives $\varphi < \varphi'$ in $[0, 2\pi)$ at
distance $d$, and the images of $\epsilon$-intervals around them with $\epsilon < \min(d, 2\pi - d)/2$ are
disjoint open sets of the quotient. Alternatively, the quotient is homeomorphic to the circle (@exm-quotient-circle-top),
which is compact and Hausdorff as a closed bounded subspace of the plane.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-circle-compact-test.sage`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Sets.Exercises.circle_quotient_compact_hausdorff >}}

**Sage.** `set-circle-compact-test.sage` instances `(T = 2 * Real.pi)`, `(T = 1)`, `(T = 3)`.
:::

The second exercise proves the homeomorphism announced in @exm-quotient-sphere-top. The key tool is that a
continuous bijection from a compact space onto a Hausdorff space is automatically a homeomorphism, and the exercise
assembles this from the closed-subset result of @exr-compact-closed-subset and the compactness of the rotation
group.

::: {#exr-sphere-quotient-homeomorphism}
#### $SO(3)/SO(2)$ is the sphere, topologically

Using that $SO(3)$ is compact and the sphere is Hausdorff, prove that $[g] \mapsto g \cdot (0, 0, 1)$ is a
homeomorphism from the quotient of $SO(3)$ by "same image of the pole" onto $S^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The map descends from the continuous surjective orbit map (@exm-continuous-matrix) and is injective by
construction of the relation: a continuous bijection $F$ from the quotient onto the sphere. The quotient is
compact, as the continuous image of compact $SO(3)$. A continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff
space is a homeomorphism: a closed set $C$ of the quotient is compact (@exr-compact-closed-subset), its image
$F(C)$ is compact, hence closed in the Hausdorff sphere, so $F$ sends closed sets to closed sets and $F^{-1}$ is
continuous. This is the topological content of $S^2 = SO(3)/SO(2)$, studied as a coset space in @sec-coset-spaces.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-compact-to-hausdorff-test.sage`; Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `set-sphere-homeomorph-test.sage`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Sets.Exercises.compact_to_hausdorff >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Sets.QuotientTopology.sphere_quotient_homeomorph >}}

**Sage.** `set-compact-to-hausdorff-test.sage` instances `(X = Unit, Y = Unit, f = id)`, `(X = Fin 3, Y = Fin 3, f = ![1, 2, 0])`, `(X = Bool, Y = Bool, f = not)`. `set-sphere-homeomorph-test.sage` instances `(p₀ = KaluzaKlein.Sets.Sets.northPole)`, `(p₀ = ![1, 0, 0])`, `(p₀ = ![0, 0, -1])`.
:::

The third exercise joins descent of maps from @def-quotient-set with continuity in the quotient topology from
@def-quotient-topology. A function constant on classes descends, and the exercise shows that the descended function
is continuous exactly when the original one is, which turns every periodic continuous function into a continuous
function on the circle.

::: {#exr-descend-continuity}
#### Descending maps and continuity

A map $f : X \to Y$ constant on the classes of $\sim$ descends to $\bar f : X/{\sim} \to Y$. Show that $\bar f$ is
continuous if and only if $f$ is, and apply it to $\cos : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and the circle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f = \bar f \circ \pi$. If $\bar f$ is continuous so is $f$, as a composition. Conversely, for $V$ open in $Y$,
$\pi^{-1}(\bar f^{-1}(V)) = f^{-1}(V)$ is open, which by @def-quotient-topology means $\bar f^{-1}(V)$ is open:
$\bar f$ is continuous. $\cos$ is continuous and $2\pi$-periodic, so it descends to a continuous function on
$\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z} \cong S^1$, the first coordinate of a point of the circle; the same argument makes every
periodic continuous function a continuous function on the circle, the functions of @exr-descend.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
